title: Notation
body_md:
Throughout the paper, $C$ denotes a positive constant whose value
may change from line to line. Constants may depend on the fixed
polynomial $P$ and the fixed cutoff functions, but are independent
of the averaging and scale parameters unless otherwise stated.
For nonnegative quantities $X$ and $Y$, we write $X\lesssim Y$
if $X\leq CY$. Additional dependence is indicated by subscripts,
as in $X\lesssim_{\varepsilon}Y$. Finally, $X\simeq Y$ means
that both $X\lesssim Y$ and $Y\lesssim X$ hold.

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $1\leq p_0,p_1\leq\infty$ and $0<\theta<1$. Define $p$ by
\[
 \frac{1}{p}
 =
 \frac{1-\theta}{p_0}
 +
 \frac{\theta}{p_1}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation*}
 \big(
 L_{p_0}(\mathcal M;\ell_\infty),
 L_{p_1}(\mathcal M;\ell_\infty)
 \big)_\theta
 =
 L_p(\mathcal M;\ell_\infty)
\end{equation*}
isometrically.

label: sup>inf
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{sup>inf}
Let $(f_n)_n\subset L_0(\mathcal A)_+$. Then, for every $\lambda>0$,
\[
 \Phi_{\sup}\left(
 \mathop{\mathrm{sup}^{+}}\limits_n f_n>\lambda
 \right)
 \geq
 \Phi_{\inf}\left(
 \mathop{\mathrm{sup}^{+}}\limits_n f_n>\lambda
 \right).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Zorn's lemma, choose a maximal pairwise orthogonal family
$(e_k)_k$ such that, for every $k$, there exists an index $n(k)$
satisfying
\[
 e_kf_{n(k)}e_k>\lambda e_k.
\]
Since $\varphi$ is finite and faithful, the nonzero members of this
family form an at most countable collection. Put
\[
 e=\left(\bigvee_ke_k\right)^\perp.
\]
We claim that
\[
 ef_ne\leq\lambda e
 \qquad\text{for every }n.
\]
Indeed, suppose that this fails for some $n_0$. Then the spectral
projection
\[
 e'
 =
 \mathbf 1_{(\lambda,\infty)}(ef_{n_0}e)
\]
is a nonzero subprojection of $e$ and satisfies
\[
 e'f_{n_0}e'>\lambda e'.
\]
Since $e'$ is orthogonal to every $e_k$, adjoining $e'$ to the
family $(e_k)_k$ contradicts maximality.

Consequently, $e$ is admissible in the definition of
$\Phi_{\inf}$, and hence
\[
 \Phi_{\inf}\left(
 \mathop{\mathrm{sup}^{+}}\limits_n f_n>\lambda
 \right)
 \leq\varphi(e^\perp)
 =\sum_k\varphi(e_k)
 \leq
 \Phi_{\sup}\left(
 \mathop{\mathrm{sup}^{+}}\limits_n f_n>\lambda
 \right).
\]

label: prop:borel-cantelli
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:borel-cantelli}
Let $\mathcal M$ be a $\mathrm{II}_1$ factor and let
$\mathcal U$ be a subgroup of the unitary group of $\mathcal M$
such that
\[
 \mathcal U' \cap\mathcal M=\mathbb C1.
\]
Let $(e_k)_{k\geq1}$ be a sequence of projections in
$ \mathcal A=L_\infty(G)\overline\otimes\mathcal M$ such that
\[
 \sum_{k\geq1}\varphi(e_k)=\infty.
\]
Then there exist $(g_k)_{k\geq1}\subset G$ and
$(u_k)_{k\geq1}\subset\mathcal U$ such that, for every $\ell\geq1$,
\[
 \bigvee_{k\geq\ell}
 \alpha_{g_k}(u_k^*e_ku_k)
 =1.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By homogeneity, replacing $A_r$ by $B^{-1}A_r$, we may assume that
$B=1$. By decomposing an arbitrary element into four positive
parts, it is enough to prove the required estimate for
$f\in L_p(\mathcal A)_+$.

In view of Lemma \ref{sup>inf}, it suffices to prove that
\[
 \sup_{\lambda>0}
 \lambda^p
 \Phi_{\sup}\left(
 \mathop{\mathrm{sup}^{+}}\limits_{r\in\mathcal I}A_r(f)>\lambda
 \right)
 \lesssim1
\]
whenever $f\in L_p(\mathcal A)_+$ and $\|f\|_p\leq1$.

Define
\[
 M(\lambda)
 :=
 \sup_{\substack{f\in L_p(\mathcal A)_+\\\|f\|_p\leq1}}
 \lambda^p
 \Phi_{\sup}\left(
 \mathop{\mathrm{sup}^{+}}\limits_{r\in\mathcal I}A_r(f)>\lambda
 \right).
\]
Since $\varphi(1)=1$, we have
\[
 M(\lambda)\leq\lambda^p.
\]
Thus, if $M$ is unbounded, then necessarily
\[
 \limsup_{\lambda\to\infty}M(\lambda)=\infty.
\]

Assume, toward a contradiction, that $M$ is unbounded. The standard
selection argument used in \cite[p.~78]{Bur64} provides sequences
$(a_k)_{k\geq1}$ and $(\lambda_k)_{k\geq1}$ of positive numbers such
that
\[
 \lambda_k\longrightarrow\infty,
 \qquad
 \sum_{k\geq1}a_k^p\leq1,
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{k\geq1}
 \left(\frac{a_k}{\lambda_k}\right)^p
 M\left(\frac{\lambda_k}{a_k}\right)
 =\infty.
\]

For every $k$, choose $f_k\in L_p(\mathcal A)_+$ with
$\|f_k\|_p\leq1$ such that
\[
 \Phi_{\sup}\left(
 \mathop{\mathrm{sup}^{+}}\limits_{r\in\mathcal I}A_r(f_k)>
 \frac{\lambda_k}{a_k}
 \right)
 \geq
 \left(\frac{a_k}{\lambda_k}\right)^p
 M\left(\frac{\lambda_k}{a_k}\right)-2^{-k}.
\]
It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{est1}
 \sum_{k\geq1}
 \Phi_{\sup}\left(
 \mathop{\mathrm{sup}^{+}}\limits_{r\in\mathcal I}A_r(f_k)>
 \frac{\lambda_k}{a_k}
 \right)
 =\infty.
\end{equation}

For every $k$ we may choose a pairwise
orthogonal family $(e_{k,i})_i$ such that
\[
 \sum_i\varphi(e_{k,i})
 \geq
 \Phi_{\sup}\left(
 \mathop{\mathrm{sup}^{+}}\limits_{r\in\mathcal I}A_r(f_k)>
 \frac{\lambda_k}{a_k}
 \right)-2^{-k},
\]
and such that, for every $i$, there exists
$r_{k,i}\in\mathcal I$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{est2}
 e_{k,i}A_{r_{k,i}}(f_k)e_{k,i}
 >
 \frac{\lambda_k}{a_k}e_{k,i}.
\end{equation}
Set
\[
 e_k=\sum_i e_{k,i}.
\]
Equation \eqref{est1} then gives
\begin{equation}\label{est3}
 \sum_{k\geq1}\varphi(e_k)=\infty.
\end{equation}

We now enlarge the underlying von Neumann algebra. Let
\[
 \mathcal N=\mathcal M*L(\mathbb F_2)
\]
be the reduced free product with respect to the given traces. Then
$\mathcal N$ is a finite factor containing $\mathcal M$ as a
trace-preserving von Neumann subalgebra; see
\cite{TakesakiIII}. Let
\[
 \mathcal N^\infty
 =
 \overline{\bigotimes}_{k\geq1}\mathcal N,
 \qquad
 \mathcal A^\infty
 =
 L_\infty(G)\overline\otimes\mathcal N^\infty.
\]

Let
\[
 \Pi_k
 =
 \operatorname{id}_{L_\infty(G)}\otimes\pi_k:
 \mathcal A\longrightarrow\mathcal A^\infty
\]
be the trace-preserving embedding into the $k$-th tensor coordinate.
Thus, for elementary tensors,
\[
 \Pi_k(f\otimes m)
 =
 f\otimes
 1\otimes\cdots\otimes1\otimes m\otimes1\otimes\cdots,
\]
where $m$ occupies the $k$-th coordinate. Put
\[
 e_k'=\Pi_k(e_k),
 \qquad
 e_{k,i}'=\Pi_k(e_{k,i}).
\]
Because the noncommutative parts of these projections lie in
distinct tensor coordinates and their $G$-components belong to the
commutative algebra $L_\infty(G)$, all the projections
$(e_{k,i}')_{k,i}$ commute whenever their first indices are
different.

Since $\Pi_k$ commutes with every $A_r$, equation \eqref{est2}
implies
\begin{equation}\label{est4}
 e_{k,i}'A_{r_{k,i}}(\Pi_k(f_k))e_{k,i}'
 >
 \frac{\lambda_k}{a_k}e_{k,i}'.
\end{equation}
Moreover, \eqref{est3} gives
\[
 \sum_{k\geq1}\varphi^\infty(e_k')=\infty.
\]

Let $\mathcal U_0$ be the subgroup of the unitary group of
$\mathcal N^\infty$ consisting of finite tensor products:
\[
 \mathcal U_0
 :=
 \left\{
 \prod_{j\in F}\pi_j(v_j):
 F\subset\mathbb N\text{ finite},
 \ v_j\in\mathcal U(\mathcal N)
 \right\}.
\]
Since $\mathcal N$ is a factor,
\[
 \mathcal U_0'\cap\mathcal N^\infty=\mathbb C1.
\]
Applying Proposition \ref{prop:borel-cantelli} to $(e_k')_k$, we
obtain sequences $(g_k)_k\subset G$ and $(u_k)_k\subset\mathcal U_0$
such that
\begin{equation}\label{est5}
 \bigvee_{k\geq\ell}
 \alpha_{g_k}(u_k^*e_k'u_k)
 =1
 \qquad\text{for every }\ell\geq1.
\end{equation}

Define
\[
 e_k''
 :=
 \alpha_{g_k}(u_k^*e_k'u_k),
 \qquad
 e_{k,i}''
 :=
 \alpha_{g_k}(u_k^*e_{k,i}'u_k).
\]
Every $u_k\in\mathcal U_0$ normalizes each tensor-coordinate
algebra $\pi_j(\mathcal N)$. In particular,
\[
 u_k^*e_k'u_k
 \in
 L_\infty(G)\overline\otimes\pi_k(\mathcal N).
\]
It follows that the projections $e_k''$, and hence all
$e_{k,i}''$ with distinct first indices, commute.

Using
\[
 A_r\alpha_{g_k}=\alpha_{g_k}A_r,
 \qquad
 A_r(u_k^*hu_k)=u_k^*A_r(h)u_k,
 \qquad
 A_r\Pi_k=\Pi_kA_r,
\]
we deduce from \eqref{est4} that
\begin{equation}\label{est7}
 e_{k,i}''
 A_{r_{k,i}}\!
 \left(\alpha_{g_k}
 (u_k^*\Pi_k(f_k)u_k)\right)
 e_{k,i}''
 >
 \frac{\lambda_k}{a_k}e_{k,i}''.
\end{equation}

Set
\[
 \gamma_k
 :=
 \alpha_{g_k}(u_k^*\Pi_k(f_k)u_k).
\]
Then $\gamma_k\geq0$ and
\[
 \|\gamma_k\|_p=\|f_k\|_p\leq1.
\]

Let $(\varepsilon_k)_k$ be the canonical independent Rademacher
variables on $\Omega_\varepsilon=\{-1,1\}^{\mathbb N}$.

Since $1<p\leq2$, the noncommutative space
$L_p(\mathcal A^\infty)$ has Rademacher type $p$; see
\cite[Corollary~5.5]{PX03} and also \cite{Fack87}. Therefore,
\begin{equation*}
 \left\|
 \sum_{k\geq1}\varepsilon_ka_k\gamma_k
 \right\|_
 {L_p(\mathcal A^\infty\overline\otimes
 L_\infty(\Omega_\varepsilon))}
 \lesssim
 \left(
 \sum_{k\geq1}a_k^p\|\gamma_k\|_p^p
 \right)^{1/p}
 \leq1.
\end{equation*}

Apply \eqref{L18 bound} in the finite von Neumann algebra
\[
 \widetilde{\mathcal A}
 =
 \mathcal A^\infty
 \overline\otimes L_\infty(\Omega_\varepsilon)
\]
to the self-adjoint element
\[
 F=\sum_{k\geq1}\varepsilon_ka_k\gamma_k.
\]
By the order description of the
$L_1(\widetilde{\mathcal A};\ell_\infty)$ norm, there exists
$b\in L_1(\widetilde{\mathcal A})_+$ such that
\[
 \|b\|_1\lesssim1
\]
and
\[
 -b
 \leq
 \sum_{k\geq1}\varepsilon_ka_kA_r(\gamma_k)
 \leq b
 \qquad\text{for every }r\in\mathcal I.
\]

Let
\[
 \mathcal D_0
 =
 W^*(e_{k,i}'':k\geq1,\ i\geq1)
 \subset\mathcal A^\infty,
\]
and set
\[
 \mathcal D
 =
 \mathcal D_0
 \overline\otimes L_\infty(\Omega_\varepsilon).
\]
Here,
$\mathcal D_0$ denotes the von Neumann subalgebra of $\mathcal A^\infty$
generated by the projections $(e_{k,i}'')_{k,i}$. Equivalently, it is
the weak-operator closure of the unital $*$-algebra generated by
these projections.
The algebra $\mathcal D_0$ is commutative. Indeed, for each fixed
$k$, the projections $(e_{k,i}'')_i$ are pairwise orthogonal. If
$k\neq\ell$, then $e_{k,i}''$ and $e_{\ell,j}''$ belong to distinct
tensor coordinates and therefore commute. Consequently, $\mathcal D$
is commutative.

Let
\[
 \mathbb E:\widetilde{\mathcal A}\longrightarrow\mathcal D
\]
be the trace-preserving conditional expectation. Applying
$\mathbb E$ to the preceding inequalities gives
\[
 -\mathbb E(b)
 \leq
 \sum_{k\geq1}
 \varepsilon_ka_k\mathbb E(A_r(\gamma_k))
 \leq
 \mathbb E(b)
\]
for every $r\in\mathcal I$. Notice that
$\mathbb E(A_r(\gamma_k))$ does not depend on the Rademacher
variables.

We are now in a commutative probability space. By
\cite[Lemma~1, p.~78]{Bur64} and Fubini's theorem,
\[
 \limsup_{k\to\infty}
 \sup_{r\in\mathcal I}
 \bigl|a_k\mathbb E(A_r(\gamma_k))\bigr|
 <\infty
\qquad\text{almost everywhere}.
\]

On the other hand, since $e_{k,i}''\in\mathcal D$ and
$\mathbb E$ is $\mathcal D$-bimodular, applying $\mathbb E$ to
\eqref{est7} gives
\begin{equation}\label{est9}
 e_{k,i}''
 \mathbb E(A_{r_{k,i}}(\gamma_k))
 e_{k,i}''
 \geq
 \frac{\lambda_k}{a_k}e_{k,i}''.
\end{equation}
Since $\mathcal D$ is commutative, \eqref{est9} implies
\[
 \sup_{r\in\mathcal I}
 \bigl|a_k\mathbb E(A_r(\gamma_k))\bigr|
 \geq\lambda_ke_{k,i}''
 \qquad\text{for every }i.
\]
The projections $(e_{k,i}'')_i$ are pairwise orthogonal and satisfy
$e_k''=\sum_i e_{k,i}''$. Hence
\[
 \sup_{r\in\mathcal I}
 \bigl|a_k\mathbb E(A_r(\gamma_k))\bigr|
 \geq\lambda_k\sum_i e_{k,i}''
 =\lambda_ke_k''.
\]
By \eqref{est5},
\[
 \bigvee_{k\geq\ell}e_k''=1
 \qquad\text{for every }\ell\geq1.
\]
Since $\lambda_k\to\infty$, we obtain
\[
 \limsup_{k\to\infty}
 \sup_{r\in\mathcal I}
 \bigl|a_k\mathbb E(A_r(\gamma_k))\bigr|
 =\infty
 \qquad\text{almost everywhere},
\]
which is a contradiction. This proves
\eqref{Lambdap8 bound}.

label: lem:borel-cantelli0
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:borel-cantelli0}
Let $\mathcal M$ and $\mathcal U$ satisfy the assumptions of
Proposition \ref{prop:borel-cantelli}. Let $p,q\in\mathcal A$ be
projections and let $\theta>1$. Then there exist $g\in G$ and
$u\in\mathcal U$ such that
\begin{equation*}
 \varphi\bigl(
 p\wedge\alpha_g(u^*qu)
 \bigr)
 \leq
 \theta\,\varphi(p)\varphi(q).
\end{equation*}
head: environment

label: bc1
title: Proof
body_md:
For arbitrary projections $p_1,p_2\in\mathcal A$, one has
\[
 \varphi(p_1\wedge p_2)\leq\varphi(p_1p_2).
\]
Thus it is enough to find $g\in G$ and $u\in\mathcal U$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{bc1}
 \varphi\bigl(p\,\alpha_g(u^*qu)\bigr)
 \leq
 \theta\,\varphi(p)\varphi(q).
\end{equation}

If either $p=0$ or $q=0$, the conclusion is immediate. Assume
therefore that $\varphi(p)\varphi(q)>0$. Suppose, toward a
contradiction, that \eqref{bc1} fails for every $g\in G$ and
$u\in\mathcal U$.

Let $\mathcal C$ be the closed convex hull in $L_2(\mathcal A)$ of
the set
\[
 \left\{
 \alpha_g(u^*qu):
 g\in G,\ u\in\mathcal U
 \right\}.
\]
Every $f\in\mathcal C$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{bc2}
 \varphi(f)=\varphi(q)
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{bc3}
 \varphi(pf)
 \geq
 \theta\,\varphi(p)\varphi(q).
\end{equation}
Because $\mathcal U$ is a group, $\mathcal C$ is invariant under
all transformations
\[
 f\longmapsto\alpha_g(u^*fu),
 \qquad g\in G,\quad u\in\mathcal U.
\]

The set $\mathcal C$ is a nonempty closed convex subset of the
Hilbert space $L_2(\mathcal A)$. Hence it contains a unique element
$s$ of minimal $L_2$ norm. For every $g\in G$ and $u\in\mathcal U$,
the element $\alpha_g(u^*su)$ also belongs to $\mathcal C$ and has
the same $L_2$ norm as $s$. By uniqueness,
\begin{equation}\label{bc4}
 s=\alpha_g(u^*su)
 \qquad
 \text{for all }g\in G,\ u\in\mathcal U.
\end{equation}
Taking $u=1$ in \eqref{bc4}, we obtain
\[
 \alpha_g(s)=s
 \qquad\text{for every }g\in G.
\]
The fixed-point algebra of the translation action on
\[
 \mathcal A=L_\infty(G)\overline\otimes\mathcal M
\]
is $1\otimes\mathcal M$, which we identify with $\mathcal M$.
Therefore, $s\in\mathcal M$.
Taking $g=e$ in \eqref{bc4}, we further obtain
\[
 u^*su=s
 \qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal U.
\]
Equivalently, $us=su$ for every $u\in\mathcal U$, and hence
\[
 s\in\mathcal U'\cap\mathcal M=\mathbb C1.
\]
Thus $s=c1$ for some scalar $c$.

By \eqref{bc2},
\[
 c=\varphi(q).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \varphi(ps)=\varphi(p)\varphi(q),
\]
contradicting \eqref{bc3}, since $\theta>1$ and
$\varphi(p)\varphi(q)>0$. This proves the lemma.

title: Proof
body_md:
Put
\[
 p_k=e_k^\perp,
 \qquad k\geq1.
\]
Since
\[
 \sum_{k\geq1}\varphi(e_k)=\infty,
\]
then
\[
 \prod_{k\geq m}\varphi(p_k)
 =
 \prod_{k\geq m}\bigl(1-\varphi(e_k)\bigr)
 =0
 \qquad\text{for every }m\geq1.
\]

We divide $\mathbb N$ into successive finite intervals
\[
 I_j=\{N_j,N_j+1,\ldots,N_{j+1}-1\},
 \qquad j\geq1,
\]
chosen so that
\begin{equation*}
 \prod_{k\in I_j}\varphi(p_k)\leq2^{-j-1}.
\end{equation*}
For each $j$, choose numbers $\theta_{j,k}>1$, $k\in I_j$, such
that
\[
 \prod_{k\in I_j}\theta_{j,k}\leq2.
\]

Fix a block $I_j$. Applying Lemma
\ref{lem:borel-cantelli0} successively within this finite block, we
can choose $g_k\in G$ and $u_k\in\mathcal U$, $k\in I_j$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{bc:block-meet}
 \varphi\left(
 \bigwedge_{k\in I_j}
 \alpha_{g_k}(u_k^*p_ku_k)
 \right)
 \leq
 \left(\prod_{k\in I_j}\theta_{j,k}\right)
 \left(\prod_{k\in I_j}\varphi(p_k)\right)
 \leq2^{-j}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, after the first $m$ projections have been chosen, apply
Lemma \ref{lem:borel-cantelli0} with $p$ equal to their meet and
$q$ equal to the next projection.

For $\ell\geq1$, set
\[
 F_\ell
 :=
 \bigwedge_{k\geq\ell}
 \alpha_{g_k}(u_k^*p_ku_k).
\]
For every block $I_j$ contained in $\{k:k\geq\ell\}$, one has
\[
 F_\ell
 \leq
 \bigwedge_{k\in I_j}
 \alpha_{g_k}(u_k^*p_ku_k).
\]
It follows from \eqref{bc:block-meet} that
\[
 \varphi(F_\ell)\leq2^{-j}
\]
for arbitrarily large $j$. Hence $\varphi(F_\ell)=0$, and the
faithfulness of $\varphi$ gives $F_\ell=0$.\\
Taking orthogonal complements, we obtain
\[
 \bigvee_{k\geq\ell}
 \alpha_{g_k}(u_k^*e_ku_k)
 =1
 \qquad\text{for every }\ell\geq1.
\]
This proves Proposition \ref{prop:borel-cantelli}.

label: prop:rep
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:rep}
Let $q\geq2$ be an integer and let $0\leq a_i\leq\mathbf 1$ for
$i\in I$. Then
\[
    \Sigma_{\mathrm{rep}}
 =
 \sum_{\substack{
 j_1,\ldots,j_q\in I\\
 \exists\,1\leq r<s\leq q\ \text{such that }j_r=j_s
 }}
 \tau(a_{j_1}\cdots a_{j_q})
\]
satisfies
\[
    |\Sigma_{\mathrm{rep}}|
    \lesssim_q
    \left\|
        \sum_{i\in I} a_i
    \right\|_{q-1}^{q-1}.
\]

label: lem: q to q-1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: q to q-1}
Let $d\ge2$, let $(a_i)_{i\in I}\subset L_\infty^+(\mathcal{N})$
satisfy $0\le a_i\le1$, and let
$h_1,\ldots,h_d\in L_\infty(\mathcal{N})$. Suppose that
\[
    \frac{d-1}{r}+\sum_{s=1}^d\frac1{r_s}=1,
    \qquad
    1\le r,r_1,\ldots,r_d\le\infty.
\]
Then
\[
    \left|
    \tau\left(
        \sum_{i\in I}
        a_i h_1 a_i h_2\cdots a_i h_d
    \right)
    \right|
    \le
    \left\|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\right\|_r^{d-1}
    \prod_{s=1}^d\|h_s\|_{r_s}.
\]
head: environment

label: Mobius for rep
title: Proof
body_md:
By M\"obius inversion,
\begin{equation}
    \Sigma_{\mathrm{rep}}
    =
    -\sum_{\substack{
        \pi\in\mathcal P_q\\
        \pi>\widehat{0}
    }}
    \mu(\widehat{0},\pi)\,\Psi(\pi).
    \label{Mobius for rep}
\end{equation}
Hence, it suffices to estimate \(\lvert\Psi(\pi)\rvert\) for every
\(\pi>\widehat{0}\).

To this end, denote the blocks of $\pi$ by
\[
    \pi=\{B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_m\},
\]
By the tracial property, we may assume that
\[
    B_0=\{1=b_1<b_2<\cdots<b_d\},
    \qquad d\geq 2.
\]
For each \(1\leq\alpha\leq m\), let $\bigl(\xi_i^{(\alpha)}\bigr)_{i\in I}$
be a family of independent and identically distributed random
variables, uniformly distributed over the set of
\(\lvert B_\alpha\rvert\)-th roots of unity. We also assume that the
families corresponding to different values of \(\alpha\) are
independent. By definition, for \(0\leq n\leq \lvert B_\alpha\rvert\),
\[
  \bigl|\xi_i^{(\alpha)}\bigr|=1,\qquad   \mathbb{E}\left[
        \bigl(\xi_i^{(\alpha)}\bigr)^n
    \right]
    =
    \begin{cases}
        1,
        & n=0\ \text{or}\ n=\lvert B_\alpha\rvert,\\[2mm]
        0,
        & 1\leq n<\lvert B_\alpha\rvert.
    \end{cases}
\]
Define
\[
    X_\alpha
    =
    \sum_{i\in I}\xi_i^{(\alpha)}a_i,
    \qquad 1\leq\alpha\leq m.
\]
For every \(k\in[q]\setminus B_0\), there exists a unique
\(1\leq\alpha\leq m\) such that \(k\in B_\alpha\). We denote this
index by \(\alpha_k\).

Set \(b_{d+1}=q+1\). For \(1\leq i\leq d\), define
\[
    H_i
    =
    \begin{cases}
        \displaystyle
        \prod_{r=b_i+1}^{b_{i+1}-1}X_{\alpha_r},
        & b_{i+1}>b_i+1,\\[4mm]
        1,
        & b_{i+1}=b_i+1,
    \end{cases}
\]
Expanding the products and using independence, we obtain
\[
    \mathbb{E}\,
    \tau\left(
        \sum_k
        a_kH_1a_kH_2\cdots a_kH_d
    \right)
    =
    \Psi(\pi),
\]
Indeed, let
\[
 J=[q]\setminus B_0.
\]
For every $r\in J$, introduce an index $j_r\in I$. Expanding the
definition of the operators $H_1,\ldots,H_d$, while preserving the
original order of the positions $1,\ldots,q$, gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{k\in I}a_kH_1a_kH_2\cdots a_kH_d
 =
 \sum_{k\in I}
 \sum_{(j_r)_{r\in J}\in I^J}
 \left(
 \prod_{r\in J}
 \xi_{j_r}^{(\alpha_r)}
 \right)
 a_{i_1}a_{i_2}\cdots a_{i_q},
\end{align*}
where the multi-index
$\mathbf i=(i_1,\ldots,i_q)$ is defined by
\[
 i_r
 =
 \begin{cases}
  k,&r\in B_0,\\
  j_r,&r\in J.
 \end{cases}
\]
Thus,
\begin{align}
 &\mathbb E\,
 \tau\left(
 \sum_{k\in I}a_kH_1a_kH_2\cdots a_kH_d
 \right)
 =
 \sum_{k\in I}
 \sum_{(j_r)_{r\in J}\in I^J}
 \mathbb E\left(
 \prod_{r\in J}
 \xi_{j_r}^{(\alpha_r)}
 \right)
 \tau(a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_q}).
 \label{eq:expectation-expansion}
\end{align}

We now compute the scalar expectation. Since the random families
corresponding to distinct blocks $B_\alpha$ are independent,
\[
 \mathbb E\left(
 \prod_{r\in J}\xi_{j_r}^{(\alpha_r)}
 \right)
 =
 \prod_{\alpha=1}^m
 \mathbb E\left(
 \prod_{r\in B_\alpha}
 \xi_{j_r}^{(\alpha)}
 \right).
\]
For every $t\in I$, define
\[
 n_{\alpha,t}
 =
 \#\{r\in B_\alpha:j_r=t\}.
\]
Then
\[
 \sum_{t\in I}n_{\alpha,t}=|B_\alpha|
\]
and, by independence of the random variables
$(\xi_t^{(\alpha)})_{t\in I}$,
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E\left(
 \prod_{r\in B_\alpha}\xi_{j_r}^{(\alpha)}
 \right)=
 \prod_{t\in I}
 \mathbb E\left[
 \bigl(\xi_t^{(\alpha)}\bigr)^{n_{\alpha,t}}
 \right].
\end{align*}
It follows that
\[
 \mathbb E\left(
 \prod_{r\in B_\alpha}\xi_{j_r}^{(\alpha)}
 \right)
 =
 \begin{cases}
  1,&j_r=j_{r'}\text{ for all }r,r'\in B_\alpha,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \mathbb E\left(
 \prod_{r\in J}\xi_{j_r}^{(\alpha_r)}
 \right)
 =
 \mathbf 1_{\{
 i_r=i_{r'}\text{ whenever }r,r'
 \text{ belong to the same block of }\pi
 \}}.
\]
Therefore, \eqref{eq:expectation-expansion} becomes
\begin{align}\label{explica}
 \mathbb E\,
 \tau\left(
 \sum_{k\in I}a_kH_1a_kH_2\cdots a_kH_d
 \right)
 &=
 \sum_{\substack{\mathbf i\in I^q\\
 i_r=i_{r'}\text{ whenever }r,r'
 \text{ lie in the same block of }\pi}}
 \tau(a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_q})\\\nonumber
 &\quad=
 \sum_{\substack{\mathbf i\in I^q\\
 \pi(\mathbf i)\geq\pi}}
 \tau(a_{i_1}\cdots a_{i_q})=\Psi(\pi).
\end{align}



On the other hand, put $A=\sum_{i\in I}a_i$. Since, we clearly have that
$\left[\begin{array}{cc} A & X_\alpha \\ X_\alpha ^*& A\end{array}\right]\geq 0$ as it  is a sum of positive elements.
We deduce that $\|X_\alpha\|_{q-1}\leq \|A\|_{q-1}$.


For \(1\le i\le d\), let $n_i:=b_{i+1}-b_i-1$ and define
\[
    p_i
    :=
    \begin{cases}
        \dfrac{q-1}{n_i}, & n_i\ge 1,\\[2mm]
        \infty, & n_i=0.
    \end{cases}
\]
By H\"older's inequality,
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \|H_i\|_{p_i}
    &\le
    \prod_{r=b_i+1}^{b_{i+1}-1}
    \left\|
        X_{\alpha_r}
    \right\|_{q-1}\leq
    \|A\|_{q-1}^{n_i}.
\end{aligned}
\]
When $n_i=0$, this means simply that $H_i=\mathbf 1$ and
$\|H_i\|_\infty=1$. Moreover,
\[
    \sum_{i=1}^d n_i=q-d,
    \qquad
    \frac{d-1}{q-1}+\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{1}{p_i}=1.
\]
Lemma \ref{lem: q to q-1}, applied with $r=q-1$, therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
    \left|
    \tau\left(
        \sum_k
        a_kH_1a_kH_2\cdots a_kH_d
    \right)
    \right|
    &\le
    \|A\|_{q-1}^{d-1}
    \prod_{i=1}^d\|H_i\|_{p_i}\leq
    \|A\|_{q-1}^{q-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking expectation, we conclude that
\[
\begin{aligned}
    |\Psi(\pi)|
    \le
    \mathbb{E}
    \left|
    \tau\left(
        \sum_k
        a_kH_1a_kH_2\cdots a_kH_d
    \right)
    \right|\lesssim_q
    \|A\|_{q-1}^{q-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining this estimate with \eqref{Mobius for rep} and using that
$\mathcal P_q$ is finite, we obtain
\[
    |\Sigma_{\mathrm{rep}}|
    \lesssim_q
    \left\|
        \sum_{i\in I} a_i
    \right\|_{q-1}^{q-1}.
\]

label: holder 2
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $f_k=a_k$. We divide the argument into three steps. In the
first two steps, $d=2$. For arbitrary scalars
$\gamma_k\in\mathbb T$, we prove the slightly stronger estimate
\begin{equation}\label{holder 2}
 \left|\tau\left(\sum_k\gamma_kf_kh_1f_kh_2\right)\right|
 \leq
 \left\|\sum_kf_k\right\|_r
 \|h_1\|_{r_1}\|h_2\|_{r_2}.
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 1: the self-adjoint case.}
Assume first that $h_1$ and $h_2$ are self-adjoint. Let
$\mathcal M_i$ be the von Neumann sub-algebra generated by $h_i$, $i=1,2$, and define
\[
 \Psi_\gamma(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)
 =
 \tau\left(\sum_k\gamma_kf_k\alpha_1f_k\alpha_2\right),
 \qquad \alpha_i\in\mathcal M_i.
\]
 By a step function of $h_i$, we mean an operator of
the form
\begin{align}\label{step function}
 \beta_i
 =
 \sum_j c_j^{(i)}
 \mathbf1_{\Delta_j^{(i)}}(h_i),
\end{align}
where the sets $\Delta_j^{(i)}\subset\mathbb R$ are pairwise
disjoint Borel sets and $c_j^{(i)}\in\mathbb C$.
If $\alpha_i$ is a step function of $h_i$ of form \eqref{step function}, then
\begin{align*}
 \Psi_\gamma(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)
 =
 \sum_{k,j,\ell}
 \gamma_kc_j^{(1)}c_\ell^{(2)}
 \tau\left(
 f_k\mathbf1_{\Delta_j^{(1)}}(h_1)
 f_k\mathbf1_{\Delta_\ell^{(2)}}(h_2)
 \right).
\end{align*}
Moreover,
\begin{align*}
\tau\left(
 f_k\mathbf1_{\Delta_j^{(1)}}(h_1)
 f_k\mathbf1_{\Delta_\ell^{(2)}}(h_2)
 \right)
\geq0.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\[
 |\Psi_\gamma(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)|
 \leq\Psi_1(|\alpha_1|,|\alpha_2|).
\]
By spectral approximation, it is therefore enough to consider
$\gamma_k=1$ and $h_1,h_2\geq0$.

 Choose
$\theta\in[0,1]$ such that
\[
 \frac1{r_1}=\frac{1-\theta}{r'},
 \qquad
 \frac1{r_2}=\frac{\theta}{r'}.
\]
After replacing $h_i$ by $h_i+\varepsilon\mathbf 1$ and then letting
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$, we may use complex powers and consider
\[
 F(z)
 =
 \tau\left(
 \sum_k f_kh_1^{\frac{r_1(1-z)}{r'}}
 f_kh_2^{\frac{r_2z}{r'}}
 \right),
 \qquad 0\leq\Re z\leq1.
\]
The function $F$ is holomorphic in the open strip and continuous on
its boundary. By the three-lines lemma,
\[
 |F(\theta)|
 \leq
 \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|F(it)|^{1-\theta}
 \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|F(1+it)|^\theta.
\]
Using the preceding domination and H\"older's inequality, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 |F(it)|
 \leq
 \Psi_1\left(h_1^{r_1/r'},\mathbf 1\right)
 =\sum_k\tau\left(f_k^2h_1^{r_1/r'}\right)
\leq
 \left\|\sum_kf_k\right\|_r
 \|h_1\|_{r_1}^{r_1/r'},
\end{align*}
where we used $f_k^2\leq f_k$. Similarly,
\[
 |F(1+it)|
 \leq
 \left\|\sum_kf_k\right\|_r
 \|h_2\|_{r_2}^{r_2/r'}.
\]
Since $r_1(1-\theta)/r'=r_2\theta/r'=1$, this proves
\eqref{holder 2} for self-adjoint $h_1,h_2$.

\emph{Step 2: the general case.}
Write
$h_1=|h_1^*|u_1^*$ and $h_2=u_2|h_2|$. The
Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
\begin{align*}
 &\left|\tau\left(\sum_k\gamma_kf_kh_1f_kh_2\right)\right|\\
 &\quad\leq
 \left[
 \tau\left(\sum_kf_k|h_1^*|f_k|h_2|\right)
 \right]^{1/2}
 \left[
 \tau\left(
 \sum_kf_ku_2|h_2|u_2^*f_ku_1|h_1^*|u_1^*
 \right)
 \right]^{1/2}.
\end{align*}
Applying Step 1 to both factors proves \eqref{holder 2} in general.

\emph{Step 3: reduction of the general case to $d=2$.}
It remains to consider $d\geq3$.
Let $(\gamma_k)_k$ be independent random variables uniformly
distributed over the {$(d-1)$}-th roots of unity. Then
\[
 \mathbb E(\gamma_k^\ell)=0
 \quad(1\leq\ell\leq d-2),
 \qquad
 \mathbb E(\gamma_k^{d-1})=1.
\]
Independence gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_k f_kh_1f_kh_2\cdots f_kh_d=
 \mathbb E\left[
 \left(\sum_k\gamma_kf_kh_1f_kh_2\right)
 \prod_{i=3}^d\left(\sum_j\gamma_jf_j\right)h_i
 \right].
\end{align*}
For every choice of the scalars $\gamma_j$, the positive
factorization used above gives
\[
 \left\|\sum_j\gamma_jf_j\right\|_r
 \leq\left\|\sum_jf_j\right\|_r.
\]
Define $s$ by
\[
 \frac1s
 =
 \frac1{r_2}
 +\frac{d-2}{r}
 +\sum_{i=3}^d\frac1{r_i}.
\]
The hypothesis of the lemma gives
\[
 \frac1r+\frac1{r_1}+\frac1s=1.
\]
Thus we may apply \eqref{holder 2} with
\[
 h_2\left(\sum_j\gamma_jf_j\right)h_3
 \cdots
 \left(\sum_j\gamma_jf_j\right)h_d
\]
as its second operator. H\"older's inequality then yields
\[
 \left|
 \tau\left(\sum_k f_kh_1f_kh_2\cdots f_kh_d\right)
 \right|
 \leq
 \left\|\sum_kf_k\right\|_r^{d-1}
 \prod_{i=1}^d\|h_i\|_{r_i},
\]
which is the desired conclusion.

label: prop:Multi-Doob
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Multi-Doob}
Consider $\ell \geq 2$ and indices with $p>1$
\[
    \frac 1 2< p_1,\ldots,p_\ell \leq\infty, \quad  \frac1p=\sum_{k=1}^\ell\frac1{p_k}.\]
  For ${1\leq i\leq N, 1\leq k\leq \ell}$, consider $a_{i}^{(k)}\in L_{p_k}^+(\mathcal N)$
  and $\xi_{i}^{(k)}\in \mathbb C$ with $|\xi_{i}^{(k)}|\leq 1$. Define
  $X_{i}^{(k)}=\sum_{j>i} \xi_{j}^{(k)}a_{j}^{(k)}$.
Then
\[
    \left\|
        \left(
            X_i^{(1)}X_i^{(2)}\cdots X_i^{(\ell)}
        \right)_i
    \right\|_{L_p(\mathcal N;\ell_\infty)}
    \lesssim_{p_1,\ldots,p_\ell}
    \prod_{k=1}^\ell
    \left\|\sum_{i=1}^N a_i^{(k)}\right\|_{p_k}.
\]

title: Lemma
body_md:

Then, for every $\pi\in\mathcal P_{q-1}$,
\[
    \left\|
        (X_i^\pi)_{i\in I}
    \right\|_
    {L_{\frac{q}{q-1}}(\mathcal N;\ell_\infty)}
    \lesssim_{q}
    \left\|
        \sum_{j=1}^Na_j
    \right\|_q^{q-1}
\]
where the implicit constant depends only on $q$ and is independent of $\pi$, $I$,
and the family $(a_j)_{j\in I}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As before, denote the blocks of $\pi$ by
\[
    \pi=\{B_1,\ldots,B_m\},
\]
Let $\bigl(\xi_i^{(\alpha)}\bigr)_{i\in I}$
be independent families  of independent and identically distributed random
variables, uniformly distributed over the set of
\(\lvert B_\alpha\rvert\)-th roots of unity ($1\leq \alpha\leq m$). Define
\[
    X^{(k)}_i
    =
    \sum_{j>i}\xi_j^{(\pi(k))}a_j,
    \qquad 1\leq k \leq q-1,
  \]
  where $\pi(k)$ is the block so that $k\in B_{\pi(k)}$.
  We already explained in \eqref{explica} that
$$\mathbb E \Big(X_i^{(1)}... X_i^{(q-1)}\Big)=
 \sum_{\substack{\mathbf j\in [i+1,N]^{q-1}\\
 \pi(\mathbf j)\geq\pi}}
 a_{j_1}\cdots a_{j_{q-1}}=X^{\pi}_i.$$
 The conclusion follows directly from Proposition \ref{prop:Multi-Doob} and the fact that $L_p(\mathcal N;\ell_\infty)$ is a normed space.

label: lem:multi-doob
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:multi-doob}
Let $(\mathcal A_n,\mathbb E_n)_n$ be an increasing filtration in a normal
semifinite tracial von Neumann algebra $(\mathcal A,\varphi)$. Let
\[
    a_n\in L_r(\mathcal A_n),
    \qquad
    x^{(j)}\in L_{p_j}(\mathcal A),
    \qquad
    x_n^{(j)}=\mathbb E_n(x^{(j)}).
\]
Then
\[
    \left\|
        \bigl(a_nx_n^{(1)}\cdots x_n^{(k)}\bigr)_n
    \right\|_{L_q(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty^c)}
    {\lesssim_{r,p_1,\dotsm,p_k}}
    \left\|(a_n)_n\right\|_{L_r(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty^c)}
    \prod_{j=1}^k\|x^{(j)}\|_{p_j},
\]
where
\[
    \frac1q=\frac1r+\sum_{j=1}^k\frac1{p_j},
    \qquad q>2,
    \qquad 2< r,p_1,\ldots,p_k\leq\infty.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $k=1$,
write $x=x^{(1)}$ and $p=p_1$, and fix $\varepsilon>0$. By the order characterization of
$L_{r/2}(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty)$, there exists
$A_{\varepsilon}\in L_{r/2}(\mathcal A)_+$ such that
\[
    a_n^*a_n\leq A_{\varepsilon}
    \qquad\text{for every }n,
\]
and
\[
    \|A_{\varepsilon}\|_{r/2}^{1/2}
    \leq
    \left\|(a_n)_n\right\|_{L_r(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty^c)}
    +\varepsilon.
\]
Since $a_n\in\mathcal A_n$, the bimodule property and Kadison's inequality give
\[
    x_n^*a_n^*a_nx_n
    =
    \mathbb E_n(a_nx)^*\mathbb E_n(a_nx)
    \leq
    \mathbb E_n(x^*a_n^*a_nx)
    \leq
    \mathbb E_n(x^*A_{\varepsilon}x).
\]
Therefore by the noncommutative Doob maximal inequality,
\begin{align*}
    \left\|
        (a_nx_n)_n
    \right\|_{L_q(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty^c)}^2
    \leq
    \left\|
        \bigl(\mathbb E_n(x^*A_{\varepsilon}x)\bigr)_n
    \right\|_{L_{q/2}(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty)}
    \lesssim_q
    \|x^*A_{\varepsilon}x\|_{q/2}
   \leq
    \|A_{\varepsilon}\|_{r/2}\|x\|_p^2.
\end{align*}
Taking square roots and letting $\varepsilon\to0$, we obtain
\[
    \left\|
        (a_nx_n)_n
    \right\|_{L_q(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty^c)}
    \lesssim_q
    \left\|(a_n)_n\right\|_{L_r(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty^c)}
    \|x\|_p.
\]
The general case follows immediately by iteration. Indeed, let
\[
 \frac1{q_j}
 =
 \frac1r+\sum_{\ell=1}^j\frac1{p_\ell},
 \qquad
 b_n^{(j)}
 =
 a_nx_n^{(1)}\cdots x_n^{(j)}.
\]
Since $q_j\geq q>2$, repeatedly applying the case $k=1$ to
$b_n^{(j-1)}x_n^{(j)}$ yields the desired estimate.

label: prop:Multi-Doob-mart
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Multi-Doob-mart}
   Let $(\mathcal A_n,\mathbb E_n)_n$ be an increasing filtration in a normal semifinite
tracial von Neumann algebra $(\mathcal A,\varphi)$. Let $d\geq 2$ and $1<p<\infty$ with
\[
    \frac1p=\sum_{r=1}^d\frac1{p_r}, \quad  1<p_1,\ldots,p_d\leq\infty.
\]
For each \(1\leq r\leq d\), let
\[
    x^{(r)}\in L_{p_r}(\mathcal A),
    \qquad
    x_n^{(r)}=\mathbb E_n\bigl(x^{(r)}\bigr).
\]
Then
\[
    \left\|
        \left(
            x_n^{(1)}x_n^{(2)}\cdots x_n^{(d)}
        \right)_n
    \right\|_{L_p(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty)}
    \lesssim_{p_1,\ldots,p_d}
    \prod_{r=1}^d
    \left\|x^{(r)}\right\|_{p_r}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $1\leq m\leq d$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$ such that
\[
 \frac1{2p}
 =
 \sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac1{p_j}
 +
 \frac{\theta}{p_m}
 =
 \frac{1-\theta}{p_m}
 +
 \sum_{j=m+1}^d\frac1{p_j}.
\]
Assume first that $0<\theta<1$. By loosing at most a  factor 4, we can assume that $x^{(m)}\geq 0$. Note also that $p_j\leq 2$ for at most  one single $p_j$ and if this occurs then $j=m$.


                                                                  
Put \[ b_n = x_n^{(1)}\cdots x_n^{(m-1)} {x_n^{(m)}}^\theta, \qquad  c_n = {x_n^{(m)}}^{1-\theta} x_n^{(m+1)}\cdots x_n^{(d)}.\]
Then
\[
 x_n^{(1)}\cdots x_n^{(d)}=b_nc_n.
\]

We apply Lemma \ref{lem:multi-doob} to $c_n$ and $b_n^*$ for $q=2p>2$.
As $p_j>2$ for $j\neq m$, it suffices to prove that
$\|({x_n^{(m)}}^{2\eta})\|_{L_{p_m/(2\eta)}(\mathcal N;\ell_\infty)}\lesssim \|x^{(m)}\|_{p_m}^{2\eta}$ for $\eta=\theta$ or $1-\theta$.

If $\eta>1/2$, by operator convexity, we have $0\leq ({x_n^{(m)}}^{2\eta})\leq \mathbb E_n \Big({x^{(m)}}^{2\eta}\Big)$. But ${x^{(m)}}^{2\eta}\in L_{p_m/(2\eta)}(\mathcal N)$ by construction and we can use the Doob inequality for the index
$p_m/(2\eta)>1$ to conclude.

If $\eta\leq 1/2$, we first apply the Doob inequality for the index $p_m$, so
$0\leq x_n^{(m)}\leq a$ for some $a\in L_{p_m}(\mathcal N)$ with $\|a\|_{p_m}\lesssim \|x^{(m)}\|_{p_m}$. By operator monotony,
$0\leq {x_n^{(m)}}^{2\eta}\leq a^{2\eta}$ and we are done.

Therefore, we have shown
\[
 \|(b_n)_n\|_{L_{2p}(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty^r)}
 \lesssim
 \prod_{j=1}^{m-1}\|x^{(j)}\|_{p_j}
 \|x^{(m)}\|_{p_m}^{\theta}, \quad
 \|(c_n)_n\|_{L_{2p}(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty^c)}
 \lesssim
 \|x^{(m)}\|_{p_m}^{1-\theta}
 \prod_{j=m+1}^{d}\|x^{(j)}\|_{p_j}.
\]
Hence, by the factorization characterization of
$L_p(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty)$,
\begin{align*}
 \left\|
  \bigl(x_n^{(1)}\cdots x_n^{(d)}\bigr)_n
 \right\|_{L_p(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty)}
 &\leq
 \|(b_n)_n\|_{L_{2p}(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty^r)}
 \|(c_n)_n\|_{L_{2p}(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty^c)}
 \lesssim
 \prod_{j=1}^d\|x^{(j)}\|_{p_j}.
\end{align*}

If $\theta=0$ all the indices $p_j>2$ and we can  take
\[
 b_n=x_n^{(1)}\cdots x_n^{(m-1)},
 \qquad
 c_n=x_n^{(m)}\cdots x_n^{(d)}.
\]
Similarly if $\theta=1$, we take
\[
 b_n=x_n^{(1)}\cdots x_n^{(m)},
 \qquad
 c_n=x_n^{(m+1)}\cdots x_n^{(d)}.
\]
The same argument, without fractional powers, proves the corresponding
endpoint estimates.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $N\geq 1$. We consider the von Neumann algebra $\mathcal A=M_{N+1}(\mathcal N)$ with its natural trace. It has a filtration given by $\mathcal A_n=M_{n+1}(\mathcal N)\oplus \mathcal N^{N-n}$ for $1\leq n\leq N$.

  We apply Proposition \ref{prop:Multi-Doob-mart} with $d=2\ell$ and the indices
  $2p_1, 2p_1, 2p_2, 2p_2, ..., 2p_\ell,2p_\ell>1$. We choose for $m=1,...,\ell$
  $$x^{(2m-1)}= \sum_{j=1}^N (a_{N-j+1}^{(m)})^{1/2}\otimes e_{1,j+1}, \qquad      x^{(2m)}=\sum_{j=1}^N \xi^{(m)}_{N-j+1}(a_{N-j+1}^{(m)})^{1/2}\otimes e_{j+1,1}.$$
  Easy computations gives that
  $\mathbb E_n x^{(2m-1)}\mathbb E_n x^{(2m)}= \sum_{j> N-n} \xi_j^{(m)}
  a_j^{(m)} \otimes e_{1,1}$ and we have that
  $\|x^{(2m)}\|_{2p_m}\|x^{(2m-1)}\|_{2p_m}=\|\sum_i a_i\|_{p_m}$. The
  conclusion of Proposition \ref{prop:Multi-Doob-mart} is exactly what
  we are looking at by noticing that for a sequence $(x_n)$ in $L_p(\mathcal N)$ its
  $L_p(\mathcal N;\ell_\infty)$-norm is the same as that of $(x_n\otimes e_{1,1})$
  in $L_p(\mathcal A;\ell_\infty)$.
head: environment

label: extreme case
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{extreme case}
  Using that $x\mapsto x^\theta$ is operator monotone for $0<\theta<1$, one can easily deduce from Proposition  \ref{prop:Multi-Doob-mart} that for $a_i\in L_p^+(\mathcal N)$, and $r>0$ provided that $p>r$, we have
  \begin{align}\label{ai} \|\Big((\sum_{j>i} a_j)^r\Big)_i\|_{L_{p/r}(\mathcal N;\ell_\infty)}\lesssim_{p,r} \|\sum _i a_i\|_p.\end{align}
    It is false in general that for $r>1$, one has, for $a_i\geq 0$,
  $$\|(a_i^r)_{i\in I}\|_
    {L_p(\mathcal N;\ell_\infty)}\lesssim_{p,r} \|(a_i)_{i\in I}\|_
    {L_{rp}(\mathcal N;\ell_\infty)}^r.$$
    One can see it easily for $r=2$ by taking $\mathcal N=M_N$, $a=N e_{1,1} +Id$ and
    $I=\{b\in M_N^+ \,|\, 0\leq b\leq a\}$. If $A$ is such that
    $0\leq b^2\leq A$, then $A\geq N/4 Id$. This would give

label: Key1-es2
title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, we may assume that
$N_0=2^{k_0}$ for some sufficiently large integer $k_0$. Recall from
Section~\ref{pre} that
\[
 \mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N)
 =
 \ell_\infty(\mathbb Z)\overline\otimes\mathcal N,
\]
equipped with the tensor-product trace. As in
\cite[Section~4.2]{CHW24}, it suffices to prove that
\begin{equation}\label{Key1-es2}
 \left\|
 \bigl(f*K_{2^k}\bigr)_{k_0<k<2k_0}
 \right\|_{L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
 \lesssim_{p,P}(\log k_0)
 \|f\|_{L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N))}
\end{equation}
for every finitely supported $\mathcal S(\mathcal N)_+$-valued function $f$ on
$\mathbb Z$. By classical cutting arguments, we can assume that $\mathcal N$ is finite and its trace is normalized.

Fix $f$ and $k_0$. Since $f$ is finitely supported, the norms in
\eqref{Key1-es2} will not change if we replace $\mathbb Z$ by a a large
finite cyclic group {\color{blue}$\mathbb Z_N$} (keeping the same formal definition
for $K$) equipped with the counting measure. By homogeneity, we can consider the normalized counting measure and it is therefore enough to prove
\begin{equation*}
 \left\|(f*K_{2^k})_{k_0<k<2k_0}\right\|_
 {L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z_N}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
 \lesssim_{p,P} (\log k_0)
 \|f\|_{L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z_N}(\mathcal N))}.
\end{equation*}

For the given target exponent $p>1$, choose an integer $q>2$
such that
\[
 p_0:=\frac{q}{q-1}<p.
\]
By Theorem \ref{pro:stein extrapolation}  followed by the Marcinkiewicz interpolation theorem \cite{JX07}
with the trivial $L_\infty$-estimate, it suffices to prove for $f\in A_{\mathbb Z_N}(\mathcal N)_+$
\begin{equation}\label{Key1-es4}
 \left\|(f*K_{2^k})_{k_0<k<2k_0}\right\|_
 {L_1(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z_N}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
 \lesssim_{q,P}(\log k_0)
 \|f\|_{L_{p_0}(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z_N}(\mathcal N))}.
\end{equation}
By duality, \eqref{Key1-es4} follows once we prove
\begin{equation*}
 \left\|
  \sum_{k_0<k<2k_0}g_k*K_{2^k}
 \right\|_{L_q(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z_N}(\mathcal N))}
 \lesssim_{q,P}\log k_0
\end{equation*}
for every finite sequence $(g_k)_k$ in $A_{\mathbb Z_N}(\mathcal N)_+$ satisfying
\[
 \left\|
  \sum_{k_0<k<2k_0}g_k
 \right\|_{L_\infty(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z_N}(\mathcal N))}
 \leq1.
\]

Let $M\simeq\log k_0$, with the implicit constant to be chosen
below, and, for $1\leq i\leq M$, set
\[
 \mathcal I_i
 :=
 \left\{
  k\in\mathbb Z:
  k_0<k<2k_0,
  \ k-k_0\equiv i\pmod M
 \right\}.
\]
Here $i=M$ represents the zero residue class. Then
\begin{align*}
 \left\|
  \sum_{k_0<k<2k_0}g_k*K_{2^k}
 \right\|_q
 &\leq
 \sum_{i=1}^M
 \left\|
  \sum_{k\in \mathcal I_i}g_k*K_{2^k}
 \right\|_q.
\end{align*}
It therefore suffices to prove independently of $i$,
\begin{equation*}
 \left\|
  \sum_{k\in \mathcal I_i}g_k*K_{2^k}
 \right\|_q
 \lesssim_{q,P} 1
\end{equation*}
provided that
\begin{equation}\label{Key1-es7}
 \left\|\sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}g_k\right\|_\infty\leq1.
\end{equation}

Fix $i$ and to simplify, denote
\[a_k:=g_k*L_k\quad\mathrm{and}\quad L_k:=K_{2^k}, \qquad(k\in\mathcal I_i),
 \qquad
 L_{k_0}:=K_{2^{k_0}}.
\]
The original indices are retained. In particular, any two distinct
indices $k,\ell\in\mathcal I_i$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:M-separation}
 |k-\ell|\geq M.
\end{equation}
Thus, we want to prove
\begin{equation*}
 \left\|
  \sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}a_k  \right\|_q \lesssim_{q,P} 1.
\end{equation*}
Since each
$L_k$ is a positive probability kernel and $g_k\geq0$, we have
$a_k\geq0$. Moreover, \eqref{Key1-es7} implies
$0\leq g_k\leq\mathbf 1$, and hence
\[
 0\leq a_k=g_k*L_k\leq\mathbf 1.
\]
Thus, it remains to prove
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q-moment-Key1}
 \left\|\sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}a_k\right\|_q^q
 =
 \sum_{k_1,\ldots,k_q\in\mathcal I_i}
 \tau(a_{k_1}\cdots a_{k_q})
 \lesssim_{q,P}1.
\end{equation}
Recall from Section~\ref{combinatorial method} that the moment sum
in \eqref{eq:q-moment-Key1} is decomposed as
\begin{equation*}
 \left\|\sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}a_k\right\|_q^q
 =
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{rep}}+\Sigma_{\mathrm{inj}},
\end{equation*}
where
\[
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{rep}}
 =
 \sum_{\substack{k_1,\ldots,k_q\in\mathcal I_i\\
                   k_r=k_s\ \text{for some }1\leq r<s\leq q}}
 \tau(a_{k_1}\cdots a_{k_q})
\]
and
\[
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}
 =
 \sum_{\substack{k_1,\ldots,k_q\in\mathcal I_i\\
                   k_r\neq k_s\ \text{for all }1\leq r<s\leq q}}
 \tau(a_{k_1}\cdots a_{k_q}).
\]
For $k\in\mathcal I_i$, recall that
\begin{equation*}
 D_k
 =
 \sum_{\substack{k_2,\ldots,k_q\in\mathcal I_i\\
                  k<k_r\ \text{for all }2\leq r\leq q\\
                  k_r\neq k_s\ \text{for all }2\leq r<s\leq q}}
 a_{k_2}\cdots a_{k_q}.
\end{equation*}
By cyclicity of the trace, every ordered $q$-tuple of pairwise
distinct indices can be cyclically rotated in a unique way so that
its smallest index occurs first. Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Sigma-inj-Key1}
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}
 =
 q\sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}\tau(a_kD_k),
\end{equation}

The repeated-index term $\Sigma_{\mathrm{rep}}$ will be estimated by
Proposition~\ref{prop:rep}. To handle the distinct-index term
$\Sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}$, we replace the first factor $a_k$ in
\eqref{eq:Sigma-inj-Key1} by the positive element $b_k$ defined in \eqref{eq:bk-Key1} and
use Proposition~\ref{prop:inj term} to estimate the family $(D_k)_k$.
The error arising from this replacement will be controlled by the
following $L_2$-estimate.


\begin{lemma}\label{L_2:Lem}
Let $k_1,\ldots,k_q\in\mathcal I_i$ be pairwise distinct and suppose
that
\[
 k_1=\min\{k_1,\ldots,k_q\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation*}
 \left\|
  (\widetilde L_{k_1}-\widetilde L_{k_0})
  *(a_{k_2}\cdots a_{k_q})
 \right\|_2
 \lesssim_{q,P} k_0^{-q}.
\end{equation*}
Here, $ \widetilde L$ has kernel given by $ \widetilde L(n):=L(-n).$
\end{lemma}

The proof of Lemma~\ref{L_2:Lem} is given in the next subsection.
Assuming this lemma, we continue the proof of
Proposition~\ref{Key1-es}.
For $k\in\mathcal I_i$, set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bk-Key1}
 b_k:=g_k*L_{k_0}.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{Key1-es7},
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}b_k
 &=
 \left(\sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}g_k\right)*L_{k_0}
 \leq
 \mathbf 1*L_{k_0}
 =\mathbf 1.
\end{align*}
 And, by \eqref{eq:Sigma-inj-Key1},
\begin{align}
\left|
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}
 -q\sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}\tau(b_kD_k)
 \right|
=
 q\left|
 \sum_{\substack{k_1,\ldots,k_q\in\mathcal I_i\\
                  k_1=\min\{k_1,\ldots,k_q\}\\
                  k_1,\ldots,k_q\ \mathrm{pairwise\ distinct}}}
 \tau\left((a_{k_1}-b_{k_1})a_{k_2}\cdots a_{k_q}\right)
 \right|.
 \label{eq:structural-difference}
\end{align}
Since
\[
 a_{k_1}-b_{k_1}
 =
 g_{k_1}*(L_{k_1}-L_{k_0}),
\]
the adjointness relation for convolution gives
\begin{align*}
\tau\left((a_{k_1}-b_{k_1})a_{k_2}\cdots a_{k_q}\right)
=
 \tau\left(
  g_{k_1}
  \bigl[(\widetilde L_{k_1}-\widetilde L_{k_0})
        *(a_{k_2}\cdots a_{k_q})\bigr]
 \right).
\end{align*}
Hence, by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, Lemma \ref{L_2:Lem}, and
$\|g_{k_1}\|_2\leq\|g_{k_1}\|_\infty\leq1$,
\begin{align*}
\left|
 \tau\left((a_{k_1}-b_{k_1})a_{k_2}\cdots a_{k_q}\right)
 \right|
\leq
 \|g_{k_1}\|_2
 \left\|
  (\widetilde L_{k_1}-\widetilde L_{k_0})
  *(a_{k_2}\cdots a_{k_q})
 \right\|_2
 \lesssim_{q,P}k_0^{-q}.
\end{align*}
Since $|\mathcal I_i|\leq k_0$, the number of tuples in
\eqref{eq:structural-difference} is at most $k_0^q$. Consequently,
\[
 \left|
  \Sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}
  -q\sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}\tau(b_kD_k)
 \right|
 \lesssim_{q,P} 1.
\]
In particular using the duality
pairing between $L_q(\mathcal N;\ell_1)$ and
$L_{\frac{q}{q-1}}(\mathcal N;\ell_\infty)$,
\begin{equation*}
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}
 \lesssim_{q,P}
 1
 + q\left|\sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}\tau(b_kD_k)\right| \lesssim_{q,P} 1+ \left\|(b_k)_{k\in \mathcal I_i}\right\|_{L_q(\mathcal N;\ell_1)}
 \left\|(D_k)_{k\in \mathcal I_i}\right\|_
 {L_{\frac{q}{q-1}}(\mathcal N;\ell_\infty)}.
\end{equation*}
Put
\[
 A=\sum_{k\in\mathcal I_i}a_k.
\]Consequently, Proposition \ref{prop:inj term} implies
\[
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}
 \lesssim_{q,P}\|A\|_q^{q-1}+1.
\]
By Proposition \ref{prop:rep},
\[
 |\Sigma_{\mathrm{rep}}|
 \lesssim_q
 \|A\|_{q-1}^{q-1}
 \leq
 \|A\|_q^{q-1}.
\]
Combining the estimates for the repeated-index and distinct-index
terms, we obtain
\[
 \|A\|_q^q
 =
 \Sigma_{\mathrm{rep}}+\Sigma_{\mathrm{inj}}
 \lesssim_{q,P}
 \|A\|_q^{q-1}+1.
\]
This gives
\[
\|A\|_q
 \lesssim_{q,P} 1,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:q-moment-Key1}.

label: eq:Omega-r
title: Proof
body_md:
For $1\leq r\leq q$, put
\[
 N_r:=2^{k_r},
 \qquad
 N_0:=2^{k_0}.
\]
Let $s_r$ be positive integers to be chosen below, and let $D\geq1$.
Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Omega-r}
 \Omega_r(\alpha)
 :=
 \sum_{0\leq s\leq s_r}
 \sum_{\xi\in\mathfrak R_s}
 S(\xi)w_{N_r}(\alpha-\xi)
 \phi(10^s(\alpha-\xi))
 \phi(D^{-1}N_r^d(\alpha-\xi)).
\end{equation}

Write $\Omega_r=\sum_{0\leq s\leq s_r}\Omega_{r,s}$. Then
\[
 \widehat L_{k_r}-\Omega_r
 =
 \left(\widehat L_{k_r}-\sum_{s\geq0}\widehat L_{s,N_r}\right)
 +\sum_{0\leq s\leq s_r}
   \bigl(\widehat L_{s,N_r}-\Omega_{r,s}\bigr)
 +\sum_{s>s_r}\widehat L_{s,N_r}.
\]
By Proposition \ref{Bo89-es1}, the first term is bounded by
$CN_r^{-c_0}$. On the support of the cutoff difference, we must have
$N_r^d|\alpha-\xi|\gtrsim D$, so \eqref{eq:wdec-v2} and the
disjointness of the major arcs in each layer give
\[
 \|\widehat L_{s,N_r}-\Omega_{r,s}\|_\infty
 \lesssim_P D^{-1/d}.
\]
Moreover, \eqref{eq:Sdec-v2} gives
\[
 \|\widehat L_{s,N_r}\|_\infty\lesssim_P2^{-s\delta_d}.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 \|\widehat L_{k_r}-\Omega_r\|_{L_\infty(\mathbb T)}
 &\lesssim_P
 N_r^{-c_0}
 +\sum_{s\leq s_r}D^{-1/d}
 +\sum_{s>s_r}2^{-s\delta_d} \notag\\
 &\lesssim_P
 N_r^{-c_0}
 +s_rD^{-1/d}
 +2^{-s_r\delta_d}.
\end{align*}
Moreover, one has
\begin{equation*}
 \|\mathcal F^{-1}(\Omega_r)\|_{\ell_1}
 \lesssim_P4^{s_r};
\end{equation*}
see again \cite[Section 6]{Bo89}. Consequently, by Young's
inequality,
\begin{equation}\label{Claim1-es1}
 \| (\Omega_r\widehat g_{k_r})^\vee\|_\infty
 \leq
 \|g_{k_r}\|_\infty
 \|\mathcal F^{-1}(\Omega_r)\|_{\ell_1}
 \lesssim_P4^{s_r}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, by the Plancherel theorem and
$\|g_{k_r}\|_2\leq1$,
\begin{align}
 \|g_{k_r}*L_{k_r}-(\Omega_r\widehat g_{k_r})^\vee\|_2
 &\leq
 \|\widehat L_{k_r}-\Omega_r\|_\infty
 \|g_{k_r}\|_2
 \notag\\
 &\lesssim_P
 N_r^{-c_0}
 +s_rD^{-1/d}
 +2^{-s_r\delta_d}.
 \label{Claim1-es2}
\end{align}

Put
\[
 B_r:=(\Omega_r\widehat g_{k_r})^\vee,
 \qquad
 H:=L_{k_1}-L_{k_0}.
\]

Here is the place where non commutativity is used. We have a telescoping
identity
\begin{align}\label{telesc}
 a_{k_2}\cdots a_{k_q}
 ={}&
 \sum_{r=2}^q
 X_2^{(r)}\cdots X_{r-1}^{(r)}
 (a_{k_r}-B_r)
 X_{r+1}^{(r)}\cdots X_{q}^{(r)}
 +B_2\cdots B_q
\end{align}
where $X_l^{(r)}=a_{k_l}$ if $k_l>k_r$ and $X_l^{(r)}=B_l$ if
$k_l<k_r$. Indeed, if $k_{\sigma(2)}<\cdots<k_{\sigma(q)}$ for some
permutation $\sigma$, one starts by replacing $a_{k_{\sigma(2)}}$ by
$B_{\sigma(2)}$, then $a_{k_{\sigma(3)}}$ by
$B_{\sigma(3)}$ in the difference and so on. Since by Young's inequality,
$\|H\|_{\ell_1}\leq2$, and
$\|a_{k_j}\|_\infty\leq1$
\begin{align*}
&
 \left\|
 \bigl[
 X_2^{(r)}\cdots X_{r-1}^{(r)}
 (a_{k_r}-B_r)
 X_{r+1}^{(r)}\cdots X_{q}^{(r)}
 \bigr]*H
 \right\|_2
\\
&\quad\leq
 \|H\|_{\ell_1}
 \left(\prod_{k_j<k_r}\|B_{j}\|_\infty\right)
 \|a_{k_r}-B_r\|_2
 \left(\prod_{k_j>k_r}\|a_{k_j}\|_\infty\right)
\\
&\quad\leq
 2\left(\prod_{k_j<k_r}\|B_j\|_\infty\right)
 \|a_{k_r}-B_r\|_2.
\end{align*}
Therefore,
combining \eqref{Claim1-es1} and \eqref{Claim1-es2}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
&\left\|
 (a_{k_2}\cdots a_{k_q})*(L_{k_1}-L_{k_0})
 \right\|_2
\notag\\
&\quad\lesssim_P
 \sum_{r=2}^q
 4^{s_2+\cdots+s_{r-1}}
 \left(
 N_r^{-c_0}
 +s_rD^{-1/d}
 +2^{-s_r\delta_d}
 \right)
 +
 \left\|
 (B_2\cdots B_q)*(L_{k_1}-L_{k_0})
 \right\|_2.
\end{align*}

Choose constants $c_2,\ldots,c_q>0$ successively, depending only on
$q$ and $P$, sufficiently rapidly increasing, such that if we put
\[
 s_r=\lceil c_r\log k_0\rceil,
\]
then  for every $2\leq r\leq q$,
\[
 4^{s_2+\cdots+s_{r-1}}2^{-s_r\delta_d}
 \leq k_0^{-q-1}.
\]
It follows, for some $c=c(q,P)>0$, that
\begin{align*}
&\sum_{r=2}^q
 4^{s_2+\cdots+s_{r-1}}
 \left(
  N_r^{-c_0}
  +s_rD^{-1/d}
  +2^{-s_r\delta_d}
 \right)
\notag
&\lesssim_{q,P}
 k_0^{-q}
 +k_0^c\left(N_2^{-c_0}+D^{-1/d}\right).
\end{align*}

Let $\Theta$ denote the support of the Fourier transform of
$B_2\cdots B_q$. From \eqref{eq:Omega-r}, $\Theta$ is contained in a
$C_qDN_2^{-d}$-neighborhood of rational points with denominators at
most $2^{C_qs_q}$. Since $s_q\simeq_{q,P}\log k_0$, for all
sufficiently large $k_0$ we have
\[
 2^{C_qs_q}<N_0^\delta
\]
for a suitably small $\delta>0$. With the polynomial choice of $D$
made below, choose the implicit constant in $M\simeq\log k_0$
sufficiently large so that
\[
 C_qDN_2^{-d}
 <
 \min\{N_1^{-d+\delta},N_0^{-d+\delta}\},
\]
so Proposition \ref{Bo89-es1}(iii) applies to both
$\widehat L_{k_1}$ and $\widehat L_{k_0}$ on $\Theta$. Using also
\eqref{eq:wdec-v2}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \sup_{\alpha\in\Theta}
 |\widehat L_{k_1}(\alpha)-\widehat L_{k_0}(\alpha)|
 &\lesssim_P
 D\left(\frac{N_1}{N_2}\right)^d
 +D\left(\frac{N_0}{N_2}\right)^d
 +N_0^{-1/2}
 \notag\\
 &\lesssim_P
 D\left(\frac{N_1}{N_2}\right)^d
 +N_0^{-1/2}.
\end{align*}
Since the indices lie in the same residue class modulo $M$,
\eqref{eq:M-separation} gives
\[
 \frac{N_1}{N_2}\leq2^{-M}.
\]
Furthermore, \eqref{Claim1-es1} and the normalized trace give
\[
 \|B_2\cdots B_q\|_2
 \leq
 \prod_{r=2}^q\|B_r\|_\infty
 \lesssim_P4^{s_2+\cdots+s_q}.
\]
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
&\left\|
 (a_{k_2}\cdots a_{k_q})*(L_{k_1}-L_{k_0})
 \right\|_2
\notag\\
&\quad\lesssim_{q,P}
 k_0^{-q}
 +k_0^c\left(2^{-c_0k_0}+D^{-1/d}\right)
 +k_0^c\left(D2^{-Md}+2^{-k_0/2}\right).
\end{align*}
Choose
\[
 D=k_0^{100d(q+c)}
\]
and then choose the implicit constant in $M\simeq\log k_0$
sufficiently large. The last display is bounded by
$C_{q,P}k_0^{-q}$, which proves \eqref{Claim1}.

body_md:
Set
\[
 m_N(\xi)
 =
 w_N(\xi/q)\varphi(D\xi/q).
\]
Since $q\leq D$, we have
\[
 \operatorname{supp} m_N\subset(-1/2,1/2).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:continuous-v2} gives $$\big\|\big(T_{w_N(./q)}(f)\big)_N \big\|_{L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb R}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)} \lesssim_{p,P} \|f\|_{L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb R}(\mathcal M))}.$$
By Young's inequality,
\[
 \left\|(T_{m_N}h)_N\right\|_
 {L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb R}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 \lesssim_{p,P}
 \|T_ {\varphi(D./q)}h\|_p\leq  \|\hat{\varphi}\|_1 \|h\|_p.
\]
Writing $n=a+\ell q$, where $0\leq a<q$ and
$\ell\in\mathbb Z$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}m_N(q\xi-n)
 &=
 \sum_{a=0}^{q-1}\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z}
 w_N\left(\xi-\frac aq-\ell\right)
 \varphi\left(
 D\left(\xi-\frac aq-\ell\right)
 \right)\\
 &=
 \sum_{a=0}^{q-1}
 w_N\left(\xi-\frac aq\right)
 \varphi\left(
 D\left(\xi-\frac aq\right)
 \right).
\end{align*}
In the last identity, the functions on the right-hand side are
understood as functions on $\mathbb T$. Indeed, since
$\varphi(D\,\cdot)$ is supported in
$(-1/(2D),1/(2D))$, for each $\xi\in\mathbb T$ and each
$0\leq a<q$, at most one integer $\ell$ contributes to the inner
sum. Thus the last expression is exactly the multiplier appearing
in \eqref{eq:cyclic-v2}. Applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:CHW-v2} proves the result.

body_md:
\label{rem:Bourgain-Lemma41}
Let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_K\in\mathbb T$ and set
\[
 R_j
 =
 \left\{
 \xi\in\mathbb T:
 \min_{1\le r\le K}
 d_{\mathbb T}(\xi,\lambda_r)\le2^{-j}
 \right\}.
\]
Bourgain's scalar estimate \cite[Lemma~4.1]{Bo89} takes the form
\[
 \left\|
 \sup_j
 \left|
 \mathcal T_{\mathbf1_{R_j}}(f)
 \right|
 \right\|_{\ell_2(\mathbb Z)}
 \lesssim
 \bigl(\log(K+1)\bigr)^2
 \|f\|_{\ell_2(\mathbb Z)}.
\]
A natural operator-valued counterpart would be
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nc-Bourgain-Lemma41}
 \left\|
 \left(
 \mathcal T_{\mathbf1_{R_j}}(f)
 \right)_j
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 \lesssim
 \bigl(\log(K+1)\bigr)^2\|f\|_2.
\end{equation}
Bourgain used  pointwise supremum and a metric-entropy
argument.  As $L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)$ has no analogous
pointwise description and we are not aware of any tool extending metric-entropy. It is presently unclear whether
\eqref{eq:nc-Bourgain-Lemma41} holds, and this appears to be an
interesting problem in its own right.

title: Proof
body_md:
For every $k\ge4^s$,
\begin{align*}
 \widehat K_{2^k}-\widehat M_{s,k}
 =(\widehat K_{2^k}-L_{2^k})
 +(L_{2^k}-L_{2^k}^{(\le2^s)})+(L_{2^k}^{(\le2^s)}-\widehat M_{s,k}).
\end{align*}
We estimate the three resulting sequences separately.

For the first one, \eqref{eq:scalar-error-v2} gives
\begin{align*}
\left\|
 \bigl(\mathcal T_{\widehat K_{2^k}-L_{2^k}}(f)
 \bigr)_{k\ge4^s}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
&\lesssim\left(\sum_{k\ge4^s}k^{-2\sigma}\right)^{1/2}\|f\|_2\\
&\lesssim2^{-(2\sigma-1)s}\|f\|_2.
\end{align*}
Next,
\[
 L_{2^k}-L_{2^k}^{(\le2^s)}
 =
 \sum_{\substack{u>2^s\\u\ {\rm dyadic}}}\Psi_{u,2^k}.
\]
By the triangle inequality,
Lemma \ref{lem:layer-v2} yields
\begin{align*}
&\left\|
 \bigl(\mathcal T_{L_{2^k}-L_{2^k}^{(\le2^s)}}(f)\bigr)_{k\ge4^s}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 \\
&\qquad\lesssim\sum_{\substack{u>2^s\\u\ {\rm dyadic}}}u^{-\gamma}\|f\|_2
 =
 \sum_{j>s}2^{-\gamma j}\|f\|_2
 \lesssim2^{-\gamma s}\|f\|_2.
\end{align*}
The third sequence is bounded by Lemma \ref{lem:comparison-v2},
\[
 \left\|
 \bigl(\mathcal T_{L_{2^k}^{(\le2^s)}-\widehat M_{s,k}}(f)\bigr)_{k\ge4^s}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 \lesssim2^{-\gamma's}\|f\|_2.
\]
Therefore, with
\[
 \delta=\min\{2\sigma-1,\gamma,\gamma'\}>0,
\]
the triangle inequality proves \eqref{eq:error-decay-v2}.

Finally, let $s\ge2$.  For every $k\ge4^s$,
\[
 \widehat M_{s,k}-\widehat M_{s-1,k}
 =
 (\widehat M_{s,k}-\widehat K_{2^k})
 +(\widehat K_{2^k}-\widehat M_{s-1,k}).
\]
Using \eqref{eq:error-decay-v2} first at level $s$ and then at level
$s-1$, and observing that
$\{k:k\ge4^s\}\subset\{k:k\ge4^{s-1}\}$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
&\left\|
 \bigl(f*(M_{s,k}-M_{s-1,k})\bigr)_{k\ge4^s}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 \\
&\qquad\lesssim2^{-\delta s}\|f\|_2
 +2^{-\delta(s-1)}\|f\|_2
 \lesssim2^{-\delta s}\|f\|_2.
\end{align*}
This proves \eqref{eq:difference-decay-v2}.

label: prop:scalar-v2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:scalar-v2}
The parameters chosen above have the following properties:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item[\rm{(i)}] If $\theta=a/q\in\Gamma_u$, then
$q\gtrsim u$ and $|S(\theta)|\lesssim u^{-\delta_d}$;

\item[\rm{(ii)}] $\mathcal Q_u|\operatorname{supp}\vartheta_u|\ll1$;


\item[\rm(iii)] For $0<\rho'<\rho$ sufficiently close to $\rho$, set
\[
 \gamma:=\delta_d-(1+\varepsilon-\rho')>0.
\]
Then the denominators $q\leq u^{1+\varepsilon}$ occurring in
$\Gamma_u$ can be partitioned into at most
$Cu^{1+\varepsilon-\rho'}$ blocks, and the least common multiple
$Q_\Lambda$ of each block satisfies
\[
 Q_\Lambda|\operatorname{supp}\varphi_u|\ll1.
\]
                                                                                                               
                               
                                             
       
                          
                 
    
                        
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\theta=a/q\in\Gamma_u$, with $(a,q)=1$.  By definition,
\[
 q\mid\mathcal Q_u,
 \qquad
 q\nmid\mathcal Q_{u/2}.
\]
Thus
$q>u/2$, and \eqref{eq:Sdec-v2} gives
\[
 |S(\theta)|
 \lesssim q^{-\delta_d}
 \lesssim u^{-\delta_d}.
\]
This proves (i).

Next, Stirling's formula gives
\[
 \log\mathcal Q_u
 =
 A\lfloor\log u\rfloor\log(u!)
 \lesssim u(\log u)^2.
\]
Since $\kappa>1$ and
$|\operatorname{supp}\vartheta_u|\lesssim2^{-u^\kappa}$, we obtain
\[
 \mathcal Q_u|\operatorname{supp}\vartheta_u|
 \lesssim
 \exp\!\bigl(Cu(\log u)^2-cu^\kappa\bigr)
 \ll1,
\]
which proves (ii).

For (iii), divide the denominators
$q\le u^{1+\varepsilon}$ occurring in $\Gamma_u$ into blocks, each
containing at most $\lfloor u^{\rho'}\rfloor$ denominators.  The
number of blocks is at most
\[
 Cu^{1+\varepsilon-\rho'}.
\]
If $\Lambda$ is one such block, then
\[
 Q_\Lambda
 \le
 \prod_{q\in\Lambda}q,
\]
and therefore
\[
 \log Q_\Lambda
 \le
 Cu^{\rho'}\log u.
\]
Since $\rho'<\rho$ and
$|\operatorname{supp}\varphi_u|\lesssim2^{-u^\rho}$,
\[
 Q_\Lambda|\operatorname{supp}\varphi_u|
 \lesssim
 \exp\!\bigl(Cu^{\rho'}\log u-cu^\rho\bigr)
 \ll1.
\]

body_md:
By  Lemma \ref{lem:cyclic-v2} with $q=D=Q$ there, we have
$$\|(\mathcal T_{J_N}f)_N\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 \lesssim  \|f\|_2,$$ with $J_N(\cdot)=\sum_{\theta\in Q^{-1}\mathbb Z \cap \mathbb T} w_N(\cdot-\theta) \chi(\cdot-\theta)$.
 The intervals $(u-\frac 1{2Q},u+\frac 1{2Q})$ are pairwise disjoint
  when $u\in Q^{-1}\mathbb Z$. Thus the Fourier multiplier on $\mathbb Z$
  with symbol $\Gamma=\sum_{\theta\in E} c_\theta 1_{(\theta-\frac 1{2Q},\theta+\frac 1{2Q})}$ is bounded on $L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M))$ by $\sup_{\theta\in E}|c_\theta|$. Since $J_N\Gamma=H_N$ by disjointness, the Lemma is proved.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write
\[
 \Psi_{u,N}=A_{u,N}+B_{u,N},
\]
where
\begin{align*}
 A_{u,N}(\alpha)
 &=
 \sum_{\theta=a/q\in\Gamma_u}
 S(\theta)w_N(\alpha-\theta)
 \vartheta_u(\alpha-\theta),\\
 B_{u,N}(\alpha)
 &=
 \sum_{\substack{\theta=a/q\in\Gamma_u\\
                  q\le u^{1+\varepsilon}}}
 S(\theta)w_N(\alpha-\theta)
 (\varphi_u-\vartheta_u)(\alpha-\theta).
\end{align*}

For every $\theta=a/q\in\Gamma_u$, one has
$q\mid\mathcal Q_u$.  Thus all the centers occurring in
$A_{u,N}$ belong to
$\mathcal Q_u^{-1}\mathbb Z\cap\mathbb T$.  Moreover,
Proposition~\ref{prop:scalar-v2}(ii) ensures that the cutoff may be
chosen so that
\[
 \operatorname{supp}\vartheta_u
 \subset
 \left(
 -\frac{1}{2\mathcal Q_u},
 \frac{1}{2\mathcal Q_u}
 \right).
\]
Since Proposition~\ref{prop:scalar-v2}(i) gives
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\Gamma_u}|S(\theta)|
 \lesssim u^{-\delta_d},
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:packet-v2}, applied with
$Q=\mathcal Q_u$, yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:narrow-v2}
 \left\|
 \bigl(\mathcal T_{A_{u,N}}(f)\bigr)_N
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
\lesssim u^{-\delta_d}\|f\|_2.
\end{equation}

For $B_{u,N}$, let $\Lambda$ be one of the denominator blocks from
Proposition~\ref{prop:scalar-v2}(iii), and define
\[
 B_{u,N}^{\Lambda}(\alpha)
 =
 \sum_{\substack{\theta=a/q\in\Gamma_u\\q\in\Lambda}}
 S(\theta)w_N(\alpha-\theta)
 (\varphi_u-\vartheta_u)(\alpha-\theta).
\]
Then
\[
 B_{u,N}
 =
 \sum_{\Lambda}B_{u,N}^{\Lambda}.
\]
If $Q_\Lambda$ denotes the least common multiple of the denominators
in $\Lambda$, then all the centers occurring in
$B_{u,N}^{\Lambda}$ belong to
$Q_\Lambda^{-1}\mathbb Z\cap\mathbb T$.  Furthermore,
Proposition~\ref{prop:scalar-v2}(iii) gives
\[
 \operatorname{supp}(\varphi_u-\vartheta_u)
 \subset
 \left(
 -\frac{1}{2Q_\Lambda},
 \frac{1}{2Q_\Lambda}
 \right).
\]
Therefore, as before with Lemma~\ref{lem:packet-v2} gives
\[
 \left\|
 \bigl(\mathcal T_{B_{u,N}^{\Lambda}}(f)\bigr)_N
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 \lesssim u^{-\delta_d}\|f\|_2.
\]
There are at most
$Cu^{1+\varepsilon-\rho'}$ such blocks.  Hence the triangle
inequality yields
\begin{align}
 \left\|
 \bigl(\mathcal T_{B_{u,N}}(f)\bigr)_N
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 &\lesssim u^{1+\varepsilon-\rho'-\delta_d}\|f\|_2
 \notag\\
 &=u^{-\gamma}\|f\|_2.
 \label{eq:wide-v2}
\end{align}
Since $0<\gamma<\delta_d$, combining
\eqref{eq:narrow-v2} and \eqref{eq:wide-v2} proves
\eqref{eq:layer-v2}.

title: Proof
body_md:
For clarity, we divide the proof into two parts.  First, we estimate
the contribution of the rational centers which occur in
$L_{2^k}^{(\le2^s)}$ but not in $\widehat M_{s,k}$, using the decay
of $S(\theta)$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:packet-v2}.  We then estimate the
error caused by the different cutoffs at the common centers, using
the separation of the rational centers, the support properties of
the cutoffs, and the decay estimate \eqref{eq:wdec-v2}.

\medskip

\emph{Step 1: the contribution of the additional rational centers.}
We first identify and estimate the rational centers which occur in the
sum defining $L_{2^k}^{(\le2^s)}$ but not in $\widehat M_{s,k}$.  Set
\[
 \Theta_s
 =
 \left\{
 \frac aq\in\mathbb Q\cap\mathbb T:(a,q)=1,\ q\mid\mathcal Q_{2^s}
 \right\}, \quad\mathcal Q_{2^s}=(2^s)!^{A\lfloor\log 2^s\rfloor}
\]
and
\[
 \Lambda_s
 =
 \left\{
 \frac aq\in\mathbb Q\cap\mathbb T:(a,q)=1,\ q\mid Q_s
 \right\},
 \qquad Q_s=(2^s)!.
\]
By the definition of the sets $\Gamma_u$,
\[
 \{0\}\cup
 \bigcup_{\substack{u\le2^s\\u\ {\rm dyadic}}}\Gamma_u
 =\Theta_s.
\]
Thus $\Theta_s$ is the set of centers occurring in
$L_{2^k}^{(\le2^s)}$, whereas $\Lambda_s$ is the set of centers
occurring in $\widehat M_{s,k}$.  Since
\[
 Q_s=(2^s)!\mid\mathcal Q_{2^s},
\]
we have $\Lambda_s\subset\Theta_s$.

When $a/Q_s$ reduces to $a'/q$, the definition of the exponential
sum gives
\[
 S(a/Q_s)=S(a'/q).
\]
Consequently, the sum defining $\widehat M_{s,k}$ may be indexed by the reduced
fractions in $\Lambda_s$, with coefficient $S(\theta)$ at the center
$\theta$.  It remains in this step to estimate the centers in
$\Theta_s\setminus\Lambda_s$.

Let $\theta=a/q\in\Theta_s\setminus\Lambda_s$ be written in reduced
form.  Then
\[
 q\mid\mathcal Q_{2^s},
 \qquad
 q\nmid(2^s)!.
\]
For a prime $\ell$ and a positive integer $n$, we write
\[
 v_\ell(n)
 =
 \max\{\nu\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}:\ell^\nu\mid n\}.
\]
Thus $v_\ell(n)$ is the exponent of $\ell$ in the prime
factorization of $n$.  We shall also use the standard formula
\[
 v_\ell(n!)
 =
 \sum_{\nu\ge1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{n}{\ell^\nu}\right\rfloor.
\]

Since $q|\mathcal Q_{2^s}$ its prime factor are smaller than $2^s$, so
if $q\nmid(2^s)!$, there is a prime $\ell\leq2^s$ such that
\[
 v_\ell(q)>v_\ell((2^s)!).
\]
We claim that this implies
\[
 4^s\lesssim q.
\]
If $\ell>2^{s-1}$, then $v_\ell((2^s)!)=1$, and therefore
$q\ge\ell^2\ge2^{2s-2}$.  If $\ell\le2^{s-1}$, put
\[
 m=\left\lfloor\frac{2^s}{\ell}\right\rfloor\ge2.
\]
Since $v_\ell((2^s)!)\ge m$, the integer $q$ is divisible by
$\ell^{m+1}$.  Moreover, $2^s<(m+1)\ell$, and hence
\[
 \frac{q}{4^s}
 \ge
 \frac{\ell^{m+1}}{4^s}
 >
 \frac{\ell^{m-1}}{(m+1)^2}
 \ge
 \frac{2^{m-1}}{(m+1)^2}
 \ge
 \frac{2}{9}.
\]
This proves the claim.

It follows from \eqref{eq:Sdec-v2} that every such center satisfies
\[
 |S(\theta)|
 \lesssim q^{-\delta_d}
 \lesssim 2^{-2\delta_ds}.
\]
Moreover, these centers can occur only in the first part of
$\Psi_{u,N}$.  Indeed, a center in its second part must satisfy
\[
 q\le u^{1+\varepsilon}
 \le2^{(1+\varepsilon)s},
\]
which is incompatible with $q\ge c2^{2s}$ because
$\varepsilon<1$.  The finitely many small values of $s$ are absorbed
into the constant.

Let
\[
 e_{s,k}(\alpha)
 =
 \sum_{\substack{u\le2^s\\u\ {\rm dyadic}}}
 \sum_{\theta\in\Gamma_u\cap
       (\Theta_s\setminus\Lambda_s)}
 S(\theta)w_{2^k}(\alpha-\theta)
 \vartheta_u(\alpha-\theta).
\]
For each dyadic $u\le2^s$, Lemma~\ref{lem:packet-v2}
applies to the terms indexed by
$\Gamma_u\cap(\Theta_s\setminus\Lambda_s)$.
There are at most $s+1$ such values of $u$.  Therefore
\[
 \left\|
 \bigl(\mathcal T_{e_{s,k}}(f)\bigr)_{k\ge4^s}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 \lesssim(1+s)2^{-2\delta_ds}\|f\|_2
 \lesssim2^{-\delta_ds}\|f\|_2.
\]

\medskip

\emph{Step 2: the cutoff error at the common centers.}
For $\theta=a/q\in\Gamma_u$, let
\[
 \eta_\theta(\beta)
 =
 \begin{cases}
 \varphi_u(\beta),&q\le u^{1+\varepsilon},\\
 \vartheta_u(\beta),&q>u^{1+\varepsilon}.
 \end{cases}
\]
At the origin we put $\eta_0=\chi_0$.  Then the contribution of the
common centers to the difference of the two multipliers is
\[
 d_{s,k}(\alpha)
 =
 \sum_{\theta\in\Lambda_s}
 S(\theta)w_{2^k}(\alpha-\theta)
 \left[
 \eta_\theta(\alpha-\theta)
 -
 \phi\!\left(Q_s^2(\alpha-\theta)\right)
 \right].
\]
By the description of the two sets of centers in Step~1 and the
definition of $e_{s,k}$, this gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:comparison-decomposition-v2}
 L_{2^k}^{(\le2^s)}-\widehat M_{s,k}
 =e_{s,k}+d_{s,k}.
\end{equation}

We next determine the support of the cutoff difference
\[
 \eta_\theta(\beta)-\phi(Q_s^2\beta).
\]  Since $u\le2^s$, the definitions of $\varphi_u$ and
$\vartheta_u$ imply that
\[
 \eta_\theta(\beta)=1
 \qquad\text{whenever}\qquad
 |\beta|\lesssim2^{-2^{\kappa s}}.
\]
Also,
\[
 Q_s^{-2}=((2^s)!)^{-2}
 =2^{-O(s2^s)}
 \gg2^{-2^{\kappa s}},
\]
because $\kappa>1$.  Since $\phi$ equals one near zero, after
decreasing $c>0$ if necessary,
\[
 \phi(Q_s^2\beta)=1
 \qquad\text{whenever}\qquad
 |\beta|\lesssim2^{-2^{\kappa s}}.
\]
The same assertion holds for the fixed cutoff $\chi_0$ at the
origin.  Consequently,
\[
 \eta_\theta(\beta)-\phi(Q_s^2\beta)=0
 \qquad\text{if}\qquad
 |\beta|\lesssim2^{-2^{\kappa s}}.
\]
Thus the cutoff error is supported where
\[
 |\beta|\lesssim2^{-2^{\kappa s}}.
\]
For $k\ge4^s$, estimate \eqref{eq:wdec-v2} therefore gives
\[
 |w_{2^k}(\beta)|
 \lesssim2^{-k}|\beta|^{-1/d}
 \lesssim2^{-k+C_1 2^{\kappa s}}
\]
on the support of the cutoff error.

For each common center $\theta\in\Lambda_s$, define
\[
 p_{\theta,k}(\alpha)
 =
 S(\theta)w_{2^k}(\alpha-\theta)
 \left[
 \eta_\theta(\alpha-\theta)
 -
 \phi\!\left(Q_s^2(\alpha-\theta)\right)
 \right].
\]
Then
\[
 d_{s,k}=\sum_{\theta\in\Lambda_s}p_{\theta,k}.
\]
By the preceding estimate,
\[
 \|p_{\theta,k}\|_\infty
 \lesssim 2^{-k+C_1 2^{\kappa s}}.
\]
We next estimate
\[
 d_{s,k}=\sum_{\theta\in\Lambda_s}p_{\theta,k}.
\]
Since the preceding bound applies to each complete difference
$p_{\theta,k}$, it remains to control how many of these terms can be
nonzero at a fixed point $\alpha\in\mathbb T$.


For $\alpha\in\mathbb T$, set
\[
 \mathcal E_s(\alpha)
 =
 \left\{
 \theta\in\Lambda_s:
 \eta_\theta(\alpha-\theta)\neq0
 \right\}
\]
and
\[
 \mathcal F_s(\alpha)
 =
 \left\{
 \theta\in\Lambda_s:
 \phi\!\left(Q_s^2(\alpha-\theta)\right)\neq0
 \right\}.
\]
We first estimate the cardinality of $\mathcal E_s(\alpha)$.  Fix a
dyadic number $u\leq2^s$.  For the centers
$\theta=a/q\in\Gamma_u$ with $q>u^{1+\varepsilon}$, we have
$\eta_\theta=\vartheta_u$.  These centers can be written with the
common denominator $\mathcal Q_u$, and
\[
 \mathcal Q_u|\operatorname{supp}\vartheta_u|\ll1.
\]
Consequently, the corresponding translates of $\vartheta_u$ are
pairwise disjoint, so at most one of them can be nonzero at a given
point $\alpha$.
For the centers with $q\leq u^{1+\varepsilon}$, we have
$\eta_\theta=\varphi_u$.  By Proposition
\ref{prop:scalar-v2}(iii), these centers can be divided into at most
$Cu^{1+\varepsilon-\rho'}$ blocks.  Inside each block the centers can
be written with a common denominator $Q_\Lambda$, and
\[
 Q_\Lambda|\operatorname{supp}\varphi_u|\ll1.
\]
Hence the corresponding translates of $\varphi_u$ are pairwise
disjoint inside each block.  Thus, at any fixed $\alpha$, at most
$Cu^{1+\varepsilon-\rho'}$ such terms are nonzero.  Including the
single center at the origin, we obtain
\begin{align}
 \#\mathcal E_s(\alpha)
 \le
 1+
 C\sum_{\substack{u\leq2^s\\u\ {\rm dyadic}}}
 \left(1+u^{1+\varepsilon-\rho'}\right)
 \lesssim 2^{C_0s}
 \label{eq:eta-overlap-v2}
\end{align}
for some $C_0>0$, uniformly in $\alpha$.

On the other hand, the elements of $\Lambda_s$ belong to
$Q_s^{-1}\mathbb Z\cap\mathbb T$, and hence two distinct centers are
separated by at least $Q_s^{-1}$.  Since
\[
 \phi\!\left(Q_s^2(\alpha-\theta)\right)
\]
is supported in an interval of length $O(Q_s^{-2})$, these
translated cutoffs are pairwise disjoint.  Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:phi-overlap-v2}
 \#\mathcal F_s(\alpha)\leq1.
\end{equation}
Since
\[
 \operatorname{supp} p_{\theta,k}
 \subset
 \operatorname{supp}\bigl(\eta_\theta(\,\cdot-\theta)\bigr)
 \cup
 \operatorname{supp}\bigl(\phi(Q_s^2(\,\cdot-\theta))\bigr),
\]
we have
\[
 \left\{
 \theta\in\Lambda_s:p_{\theta,k}(\alpha)\neq0
 \right\}
 \subset
 \mathcal E_s(\alpha)\cup\mathcal F_s(\alpha).
\]
It follows from \eqref{eq:eta-overlap-v2},
\eqref{eq:phi-overlap-v2}, and the estimate for
$\|p_{\theta,k}\|_\infty$ that
\begin{align*}
 |d_{s,k}(\alpha)|
 \le
 \sum_{\substack{\theta\in\Lambda_s
                  p_{\theta,k}(\alpha)\neq0}}
 |p_{\theta,k}(\alpha)|\lesssim2^{C_0s}2^{-k+C_1 2^{\kappa s}}.
\end{align*}
Taking the supremum over $\alpha\in\mathbb T$, we conclude that
\begin{equation*}
 \|d_{s,k}\|_\infty
 \lesssim2^{C_0s}2^{-k+C_1 2^{\kappa s}}.
\end{equation*}
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
\left\|
 \bigl(\mathcal T_{d_{s,k}}(f)\bigr)_{k\geq 4^s}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
&\qquad\lesssim\left(
 \sum_{k\geq 4^s}
 \|\mathcal F^{-1}[d_{s,k}\widehat f]\|_2^2
 \right)^{1/2}\\
&\qquad\lesssim2^{C_0s+C_1 2^{\kappa s}}
 \left(\sum_{k\ge4^s}2^{-2k}\right)^{1/2}\|f\|_2\\
&\qquad\lesssim2^{C_0s+C_1 2^{\kappa s}-4^s}\|f\|_2.
\end{align*}
Since $\kappa<2$, we have $2^{\kappa s}=o(4^s)$.  It follows that
\[
 2^{C_0s+C_1 2^{\kappa s}-4^s}
 \lesssim2^{-C_{-1} s
}\]
for some $C_{-1}>0$. We obtain
\[
 \left\|
 \bigl(\mathcal T_{d_{s,k}}(f)\bigr)_{k\ge4^s}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 \lesssim2^{-C_{-1}s}\|f\|_2.
\]

\medskip

\emph{Step 3: conclusion.}
By \eqref{eq:comparison-decomposition-v2}, the triangle inequality
gives
\begin{align*}
 &\left\|
 \left(
 \mathcal T_{L_{2^k}^{(\leq2^s)}-\widehat M_{s,k}}f
 \right)_{k\geq4^s}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal M);\ell_\infty)}
 \\
 &\qquad\lesssim \left(2^{-\delta_ds}+2^{-C_{-1}s}\right)\|f\|_2
\lesssim2^{-\gamma's}\|f\|_2,
\end{align*}
where
\[ \gamma'=\min\{\delta_0,C_{-1}\}>0.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:comparison-v2}.

label: thm111
title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove the maximal inequality \eqref{mthm1}.
 It suffices to prove
\eqref{thm11}, namely,
\begin{equation}\label{thm111}
   \big\|(f*K_{2^k})_{k\in\mathbb N}\big\|_
   {L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
   \lesssim_{p} \|f\|_{L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N))}.
\end{equation}

Since each convolution operator $f\mapsto f*K_{2^k}$ is positive,
the standard decomposition of an arbitrary element into four
positive elements reduces the proof to the case $f\geq0$.  We first
consider $1<p<2$.  The finitely many indices $k<4$ are bounded by
$C\|f\|_p$, since $\|f*K_{2^k}\|_p\leq\|f\|_p$.  Thus it remains to
consider $k\geq4$.

Given $k\in[4^s,4^{s+1})$, where $s$ is a positive integer,
\begin{equation*}
    f*K_{2^k}=\Big(f*K_{2^k}-f*M_{s,k}\Big)+\sum_{s^\prime=1}^sf*\Big(M_{s^\prime,k}-M_{s^\prime-1,k}\Big).
\end{equation*}
Here, $M_{0,k}:=0$.
For $k\ge4$, put $s(k)=\lfloor\log_4k\rfloor$. Then
$$\Big(\sum_{s^\prime=1}^{s(k)}f*\big(M_{s^\prime,k}-M_{s^\prime-1,k}\big)\Big)_{k\geq 4}=\sum_{s^\prime=1}^{\infty}\Big(1_{k\geq 4^{s'}}f*\big(M_{s^\prime,k}-M_{s^\prime-1,k}\big)\Big)_{k\geq 4}.$$
Consequently,
\begin{align}\label{Key-es2}
    \big\|(f*K_{2^k})_{k\in\mathbb N}\big\|_
    {L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
    \lesssim(I)+(II),
    \end{align}
where
\begin{equation*}
    (I)=\sum_{s=1}^\infty
    \big\|\big(f*(K_{2^k}-M_{s,k})\big)_{4^s\leq k<4^{s+1}}\big\|_
    {L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
    (II)=\sum_{s^\prime=1}^\infty
    \big\|\big(f*(M_{s^\prime,k}-M_{s^\prime-1,k})\big)_{k\ge4^{s^\prime}}\big\|_
    {L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}.
\end{equation*}
Choose $p_0$ such that $1<p_0<p$.  By Lemma \ref{lem:M-p-v2},
\begin{equation}\label{Key-es3}
    \big\|(f*M_{s^\prime,k})_{k\ge4^{s^\prime}}\big\|_
    {L_{p_0}(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
    \lesssim\|f\|_{p_0}.
\end{equation}Hence, by the triangle inequality and \eqref{Key-es3},
\begin{equation}\label{Key-es5}
    \big\|\big(f*(M_{s^\prime,k}-M_{s^\prime-1,k})\big)_{k\ge4^{s^\prime}}\big\|_
    {L_{p_0}(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
    \lesssim\|f\|_{p_0}.
\end{equation}
The interval $[4^s,4^{s+1})$ is the union of
$[4^s,2\cdot4^s)$ and $[2\cdot4^s,4\cdot4^s)$.  Applying
Proposition \ref{Key1-es} with $N_0=2^{4^s}$ and
$N_0^2=2^{2\cdot4^s}$, respectively, and absorbing the endpoints into
the constant, we obtain the following estimate, since
$\log\log(2^{4^s})\simeq s$:
\begin{equation}\label{Key-es4}
    \big\|(f*K_{2^k})_{4^s\leq k<4^{s+1}}\big\|_
    {L_{p_0}(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
    \lesssim s\|f\|_{p_0}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, \eqref{Key-es3} and \eqref{Key-es4} give
\begin{equation}\label{Key-es6}
    \big\|\big(f*(K_{2^k}-M_{s,k})\big)_{4^s\leq k<4^{s+1}}\big\|_
    {L_{p_0}(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
    \lesssim s\|f\|_{p_0}.
\end{equation}
By Lemma \ref{lem:L2decay-v2}, for $s^\prime\geq2$ we have
\begin{equation}\label{Key-es7}
   \big\|\big(f*(M_{s^\prime,k}-M_{s^\prime-1,k})\big)_{k\ge4^{s^\prime}}\big\|_
   {L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
   \lesssim2^{-\delta s^\prime}\|f\|_{2}.
\end{equation}
The same lemma also gives, for every $s\geq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{Key-es8}
     \big\|\big(f*(K_{2^k}-M_{s,k})\big)_{4^s\leq k<4^{s+1}}\big\|_
     {L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
     \lesssim 2^{-\delta s}\|f\|_{2}.
\end{equation}
The case $s^\prime=1$ in \eqref{Key-es7} follows from Lemma
\ref{lem:M-p-v2} with $p=2$, after increasing the implicit constant.

Let $0<\theta<1$ be determined by
\[
 \frac1p=\frac{1-\theta}{p_0}+\frac\theta2.
\]
Interpolating \eqref{Key-es5} with \eqref{Key-es7}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{Key-es9}
   \big\|\big(f*(M_{s^\prime,k}-M_{s^\prime-1,k})\big)_{k\ge4^{s^\prime}}\big\|_
   {L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
   \lesssim2^{-\delta_ps^\prime}\|f\|_{p}.
\end{equation}
Similarly, interpolation between \eqref{Key-es6} and
\eqref{Key-es8} first gives
\begin{equation}\label{Key-es10}
     \big\|\big(f*(K_{2^k}-M_{s,k})\big)_{4^s\leq k<4^{s+1}}\big\|_
     {L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
     \lesssim s^{1-\theta}2^{-\theta\delta s}\|f\|_{p}
     \lesssim 2^{-\delta_ps}\|f\|_{p},
\end{equation}
where one may take any $0<\delta_p<\theta\delta$.  Combining
\eqref{Key-es2}, \eqref{Key-es9}, and \eqref{Key-es10}, and summing
the resulting geometric series, we deduce
\begin{equation*}
     \big\|(f*K_{2^k})_{k\in\mathbb N}\big\|_
     {L_p(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
     \lesssim \|f\|_p.
\end{equation*}

For $p=2$, the same conclusion follows directly from
\eqref{Key-es2}, \eqref{Key-es7}, and \eqref{Key-es8}.  Finally, for
$2<p<\infty$, interpolate the $L_2$ estimate with the evident bound
\[
 \big\|(f*K_{2^k})_{k\in\mathbb N}\big\|_
 {L_\infty(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}
 \leq \|f\|_\infty.
\]
This proves \eqref{thm111} for every $1<p<\infty$, and hence
establishes \eqref{mthm1}.

Since the maximal inequality holds in $L_p$, to prove the b.a.u. convergence for $f\in L_p$, it suffices to do it only when $f\in L_2$.  To do so, by the  the discussion in
\cite[Section~4.1]{HongWang+arXiv2026}, it suffices to prove an analog of arguments of
\cite[Proposition~4.4]{HongWang+arXiv2026}. More precisely,  it suffices to show that for  fixed $0<\varepsilon<1/4$, there is a sequence $c_J\to 0$ such that  with
\[
 \mathbb D_\varepsilon
 =
 \{\lfloor(1+\varepsilon)^k\rfloor:k\geq1\},
 \qquad
 I_i=\mathbb D_\varepsilon\cap[N_i,N_{i+1}),
\]
where $N_i\in\mathbb D_\varepsilon$ and $N_{i+1}>2N_i$ and any $f\in L_2$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quantitative-convergence}
 \frac1{J+1}\sum_{i=0}^J
 \left\|
 \bigl(f*K_N-f*K_{N_i}\bigr)_{N\in I_i}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}^2
 \leq c_J\|f\|_2^2.
\end{equation}

Fix $s\geq1$. Decompose, using \eqref{eq:LN-v2} and \eqref{eq:defLNs},
\[
 \widehat K_N
 =
 (\widehat K_N-L_N)
 +L_N^{(\leq2^s)}
 +(L_N-L_N^{(\leq2^s)}).
\]
Let $T_N^{(1)}$, $T_{s,N}^{(2)}$, and $T_{s,N}^{(3)}$
be the operators with these three multipliers, respectively.
Then
\[
 f*K_N
 =
 T_N^{(1)}f+T_{s,N}^{(2)}f+T_{s,N}^{(3)}f.
\]
For the first term, \eqref{eq:scalar-error-v2},
and Plancherel's theorem give
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{i=0}^J
 \left\|
 \bigl(T_N^{(1)}f-T_{N_i}^{(1)}f\bigr)_{N\in I_i}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}^2
 \lesssim_{\varepsilon,P}
 \left(
 \sum_{N\in\mathbb D_\varepsilon}(\log N)^{-2\sigma}
 \right)\|f\|_2^2
 \lesssim_P\|f\|_2^2,
\end{align*}
since $\sigma>1/2$.
For the third term, summing the bounds in
Lemma~\ref{lem:layer-v2} over dyadic $u>2^s$ yields
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^J
 \left\|
 \bigl(T_{s,N}^{(3)}f-T_{s,N_i}^{(3)}f\bigr)_{N\in I_i}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}^2
 \lesssim_P
 (J+1)2^{-2\gamma s}\|f\|_2^2.
\]
It remains to estimate $T_{s,N}^{(2)}$. Its multiplier is a
finite sum of terms
\[
 S(\theta)w_N(\alpha-\theta)\chi(\alpha-\theta),
\]
where $\theta$ and $\chi$ are independent of $N$.
We compare $w_N$ with the corresponding expression for the
leading monomial $a_dt^d$:
\[
 w_N^{(0)}(\beta)
 :=
 \frac1N\int_0^N
 \exp(-2\pi i\beta a_dt^d)\,dt.
\]
 Estimate \eqref{eq:wdec-v2} gives
\[
 |w_N(\beta)-w_N^{(0)}(\beta)|
 \lesssim_P
 \min\bigl\{
 |\beta|N^{d-1},(N^d|\beta|)^{-1/d}
 \bigr\},
 \qquad \beta\neq0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \|w_N-w_N^{(0)}\|_\infty
 \lesssim_P N^{-1/(d+1)}.
\]
For each fixed $\theta$ and $\chi$,
\cite[Corollary~4.8 and Remark~4.9]{HongWang+arXiv2026}
gives the quantitative maximal estimate over the intervals
$I_i$ for the multiplier
\[
 S(\theta)w_N^{(0)}(\alpha-\theta)\chi(\alpha-\theta),
\]
with a constant independent of $J$ and $(N_i)$. For the difference $w_N-w_N^{(0)}$, the same
calculation as for $T_N^{(1)}$, we have
\[
 \left(
 \sum_{N\in\mathbb D_\varepsilon}
 \|w_N-w_N^{(0)}\|_\infty^2
 \right)\|f\|_2^2
 \lesssim_{P}
 \left(
 \sum_{N\in\mathbb D_\varepsilon}N^{-2/(d+1)}
 \right)\|f\|_2^2
 \lesssim_{\varepsilon,P}\|f\|_2^2.
\]
Combining this bound with the estimate for $w_N^{(0)}$
and summing over the finitely many terms, we obtain
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^J
 \left\|
 \bigl(T_{s,N}^{(2)}f-T_{s,N_i}^{(2)}f\bigr)_{N\in I_i}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}^2
 \lesssim_{\varepsilon,P,s} \|f\|_2^2,
\]
where the constant is independent of $J$ and $(N_i)$.

Combining these three bounds, we obtain
\[
 \frac1{J+1}\sum_{i=0}^J
 \left\|
 \bigl(f*K_N-f*K_{N_i}\bigr)_{N\in I_i}
 \right\|_{L_2(\mathcal A_{\mathbb Z}(\mathcal N);\ell_\infty)}^2
 \leq
 \left(
 \frac{C_{\varepsilon,P,s}}{J+1}
 +C_P2^{-2\gamma s}
 \right)\|f\|_2^2.
\]
Letting $J\to\infty$ and then $s\to\infty$ proves
\eqref{eq:quantitative-convergence}.
The desired b.a.u. convergence now follows from the discussion in
\cite[Section~4.1]{HongWang+arXiv2026}.
This completes the proof.

body_md: If $\mathcal C$ is stochastically convex with the finiteness condition, then there is some $K>0$ such that for all $F\in \mathcal C$, $\|F\|_{\Lambda_{1}(\mathcal M_F;\ell_\infty)}\leq K$.

title: Proof
body_md:
As in  \cite{Bur64}, if the conclusion does not hold then we may find a sequence $\lambda_k\to \infty$, $a_k>0$ with $\sum a_k=1$ and $G_k=(g_{k,n})_n\in \mathcal C$ such that $\sum_{k=1}^\infty \Phi_{\rm inf}(\sup^+_na_kg_{k,n}>\lambda_k)=\infty$ and the $(G_k)$ are tensor independent.

  Let $\mathcal M_k= \mathcal M_{G_k}$ for $k\geq 1$, we can see them in a bigger $(\mathcal M,\tau)$ as they are independent. There are conditional expectations $\mathbb E_k : \mathcal M \to \mathcal M_k$. We will also use that
  independence forces the spaces
$L_2(\mathcal M_k)\cap 1^\bot$ to be orthogonal in $L_2(\mathcal M)$.

  Let $X=(x_n)_n=\sum_{k=1}^\infty
  a_kG_k$, that is $x_n=\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_kg_{k,n}$.
  To get a contraction with the finiteness condition, we
  want to show that for any projection $p\in \mathcal
  M$ with $\tau(p)=t>0$ we have $\sup_n \|px_np\|=\infty$.

 Set
  $f_k=\mathbb E_k(p)$, then $f_k-t$ has mean 0 and by independence
  $\sum_{k=1}^\infty \|f_k-t\|_2^2\leq \| p-t\|_2^2<\infty$.

  Put $p_k=1_{f_k\geq t/2}$ and $p_k^\bot=1-p_k=1_{t-f_k> t/2}$. We have $t^2/4\tau(p_k^\bot)\leq \|f_k-t\|^2$, thus $\sum_k \tau(p_k^\bot)<\infty$. This obviously implies that $I=\{k\geq 1 \;|\; \tau(p_k^\bot)<\Phi_{\rm inf}(\sup^+_na_kg_{k,n}>\lambda_k)\}$ is infinite.

  Now, since $x_n\geq a_kg_{k,n}$, we have
  \begin{equation*}\|x_n^{1/2}p\|_\infty\geq
  \|(a_kg_{k,n})^{1/2}p\|_\infty\geq \| \mathbb E_k((a_kg_{k,n})^{1/2}p)\|_\infty=\|(a_kg_{k,n})^{1/2}f_k\|_\infty.\end{equation*}
  But $f_k\geq t/2 p_k$ and they commute so $t/2p_k=f_kc$ for some contraction $c$
  and we conclude, for all $k,n\geq 1$
  \begin{equation}\label{normxn}\|px_np\|_\infty\geq t^2/4\|p_k a_k g_{k,n}p_k\|_\infty.\end{equation}

  Fix $k\geq 1$, if for all $n\geq 1$, we have
  $\|p_k a_k g_{k,n}p_k\|_\infty\leq \lambda_k$, then by definition of $\Phi_{\inf}$ in \eqref{phi_inf},  $\Phi_{\rm inf}(\sup^+_na_kg_{k,n}>\lambda_k)\leq \tau(p_k^\bot)$ and thus $k\notin I$. It follows that $\sup_n \|p_ka_k g_{k,n}p_k\|\geq \lambda_k$ for $k\in I$. Since $I$ is infinite and $\lambda_k\to \infty$, \eqref{normxn} yields $\sup_n \|px_np\|=\infty$ and the proof is over.
